title: What a mascot does: brand moments, a companion, or pressure
block path: Foundations > Illustration > Characters > The mascot's job
questions: (questions the designer answers) Does the product have a mascot or character? Does it only appear in a few moments, or does it react to the person as a personality? May it ever look disappointed or angry when someone lapses? Is it one figure, or a whole branded world?
options:
- **No mascot.** Q-img-04 `none`; warmth comes from type, color and illustration instead (DC-L05-19) [inferred].
- **A mascot in brand moments.** The current Q-img-04 `mascot` option: loading, error and empty states (Mailchimp's Freddie, Duolingo's Duo); Freddie smiles and winks but does not talk (DC-L06-12). The patterns area keeps a colorful spot or mascot to first-use empty states (DC-L19-126).
- **A companion that reacts to the person.** Mascots are not only there to make apps feel cute; they are designed to create attachment: a mascot cheering you on as if it believes in you, a little bird that grows alongside you. Duolingo's owl became a personality, and the presenter kept opening the app so as not to disappoint Duo, not for the streak number [S-L19-105]. The video names the mechanisms, anthropomorphism and the Tamagotchi effect (the attachment that forms when a digital thing appears to need you back), and notes that once people feel something for a product, leaving feels harder [S-L19-105]. It presents this as a retention tactic, not as a neutral style choice.
- **A mascot that makes people feel guilty.** Fear-based streak screens pair more urgent copy and a countdown with an angry owl that gives a sense of guilt [S-L19-105]. The video describes this rather than endorsing it, and asks whether streaks build habits or just make people afraid to stop [S-L19-105]. Not offered here: it is guilt aimed at the person, which DC-L19-37 (never at the user) and DC-L19-135 reject, and it sits beside confirmshaming and nagging in DC-L13-15's policy [inferred mapping].
- **Custom characters and a built world.** A paywall designer expects the most successful apps to be the ones polished with animations, custom character designs and world building, and cites Focus Town's Animal Crossing-like experience; the host adds that when two products compete for the same user, that polish can decide [S-L19-104] (one guest's prediction).
visual effect: A mascot in a few moments adds warmth while the rest of the UI stays neutral (DC-L06-12). A companion is built to make people attached to it [S-L19-105], so the product feels alive rather than decorated [inferred]. A guilt mascot turns a lapse into letting someone down [S-L19-105]. A built world makes the app feel like one crafted place [S-L19-104] [inferred wording].
depends on: Q-brand-01 (playful to serious), Q-brand-04 (how lively), Q-aud-02 (consumer or play), illustration style and who pays (DC-L19-75), progress and streak mechanics (DC-L19-136), tone (DC-L19-37), the deceptive-pattern policy (Q-pattern-05, DC-L13-15).
affects: empty, error, loading and success states; onboarding; streak and progress screens; celebration moments (DC-L19-130); notification copy; the illustration and animation asset list (Q-img-06).
token encoding: None (a content decision). The mascot's colors alias brand primitives like any illustration (DC-L05-19); its poses live in an asset manifest, one file per state, such as `mascot/<state>.svg` or a Lottie file [inferred names].
platform notes: None from the sources. Animated mascots ship through Q-img-06's formats (Lottie, dotLottie, Rive).
accessibility constraints: A mascot's expression never carries status on its own (DC-L06-12), and a decorative mascot is hidden from assistive tech (DC-L05-20). Mascot animations and milestone celebrations are delight motion, so they belong only to rare or first-time moments (STD-when-to-animate-03, STD-when-to-animate-09) and lose their movement under reduced motion (STD-accessibility-motion-02). A companion that reacts to lapses follows DC-L19-136's rule that a missed day is never punished, so it never takes away progress or blocks content [inferred].
default: (default + heuristic) `none` unless the brand already has a character, or is playful and consumer-facing; with a mascot, `moments` by default. A companion that reacts to the person's own progress is an explicit choice for consumer and play products [inferred scope]. Rule of thumb: the mascot may cheer, celebrate and grow with the person, and never sulks, scolds or threatens (both sides are in [S-L19-105]; drawing the line there is [inferred], in line with DC-L19-37). Check its look against who pays (DC-L19-75): cartoonish characters can miss an older paying audience [S-L19-111].
maps to:
- Q-img-04: `mascot` gains its purpose, "a character people get attached to" [S-L19-105]; new use/avoid "a mascot never guilts or shames the person: no angry mascot when they miss a day".
- New question Q-img-09 (stage 18, zoom 3; show if Q-img-04 is `mascot`): "What does the mascot do: show up in key moments, react to the person's progress, or anchor a whole branded world?" Options `moments` (default), `companion`, `world`. Guilt is not an option, because DC-L19-37 rules out guilt aimed at the person and DC-L13-15's policy lists confirmshaming beside it; Q-pattern-05, which would enforce that policy, is still Planned (the engine has no deceptive-pattern lint yet), so nothing blocks a guilt mascot automatically and the rule lives in this question's options [inferred].
- Visual sample: streak screens side by side, an angry owl with urgent copy and a countdown beside a cheering mascot and a little bird that grows with you [S-L19-105].
impact now / as it grows:
- No mascot: now, nothing to draw or maintain. As it grows, warmth has to come from other devices [inferred].
- Brand moments: now, a warm touch in a few states. As it grows, each new state raises the question of whether the mascot appears; DC-L19-126's first-use rule keeps it rare [inferred].
- Companion: now, attachment that brings people back [S-L19-105]. As it grows, every progress state needs a matching pose and reaction, and the character becomes part of what people would miss [inferred].
- Guilt mascot: now, perhaps more daily opens. As it grows, it trades trust for pressure; the video itself asks whether it builds habits or fear [S-L19-105].
- Built world: now, a polished, distinctive product [S-L19-104]. As it grows, every new feature needs art in the world's style, a continuing illustration cost [inferred].
standards: STD-when-to-animate-03, STD-when-to-animate-09, STD-accessibility-motion-02, STD-visual-details-44 (spend people's attention and trust only where it pays off), STD-visual-details-47 (decide the emotion, then reinforce it).

title: How an AI helper is pictured
questions: (questions the designer answers) If the product has an AI helper, what does it look like: a mark or shape of its own, an abstract faceless form, a cartoon character, or a realistic persona? Does it get a name and a face? How do people always know it is an AI?
options:
- **A distinct shape or mark, no face.** Primer draws bots and AI agents as squares and Atlassian uses a hexagon (DC-L05-18); this is Q-img-03 `agent-shape`. The research recommends a neutral, non-anthropomorphic voice, because human-sounding explanations lead people to overestimate what the AI can do (DC-L13-16).
- **Faceless.** Moonly tried a faceless approach for its AI astrologer; it did not appeal to its users [S-L19-111].
- **A cartoon or Disney-like character.** Also tried, and also did not appeal [S-L19-111].
- **A realistic persona.** Moonly's AI astrologer, Luna, moved toward realism after the other looks failed; the video says realism works better here but does not show or describe her final look [inferred that it is realistic]. The reason given: when people receive meaningful personal guidance, they need the entity to feel trustworthy, so realism works better [S-L19-111] (one app, self-reported, with no numbers given for the look). Differs from DC-L13-16 (a non-anthropomorphic voice) and from Q-img-03's use/avoid ("avoid using the person circle for bots").
visual effect: A distinct mark makes the AI easy to spot among people and reads as a tool (DC-L05-18). Faceless and cartoon looks did not win Moonly's users over [S-L19-111]. A realistic persona feels trustworthy for personal guidance [S-L19-111]; it can also make the AI read as a person, which is the overestimation DC-L13-16 warns about [inferred].
depends on: Q-ai-01 (whether and how AI appears), avatar shapes (Q-img-03, DC-L05-18), AI identifiers and voice (DC-L13-16), imagery style and who pays (DC-L19-75).
affects: the AI's avatar in chat, comments and mentions; its name and voice; onboarding and paywall images that feature the helper; the AI label and AI module (DC-L08-22, DC-L19-138).
token encoding: An agent shape beside the person and entity shapes, such as `avatar.radius.agent` or an agent mask asset (DC-L05-18), plus `color.ai.*` and `icon.ai` (DC-L13-16) [inferred names]. A persona's portraits are assets, not tokens.
platform notes: None from the sources.
accessibility constraints: The AI's avatar has an accessible name that says it is an AI, such as "Luna, AI astrologer" [inferred]; the AI label is text, never the look alone (DC-L13-16) [inferred]; the avatar's expression never carries status on its own (DC-L06-12).
default: (default + heuristic) Keep `agent-shape`: a mark of its own, never the person circle, with a neutral voice (DC-L05-18, DC-L13-16). A realistic persona is an explicit choice for products whose AI gives personal guidance, and then only with the AI label always beside it and a shape or badge that sets it apart from people [inferred conditions]. One app's result [S-L19-111] does not outweigh the research, so its caution holds. Rule of thumb: people never have to guess whether they are dealing with a person or an AI [inferred from DC-L13-16 and STD-visual-details-36].
maps to:
- Q-img-03: confirms `agent-shape` for products with AI actors; new option `ai-persona` ("A named AI character with a realistic look, for AI that gives personal guidance, always labelled as AI"), noted "differs from DC-L13-16; one app's evidence" [S-L19-111]; new use/avoid "never show an AI in the person circle, or as a realistic portrait without its AI label"; the AI part of the question shows when Q-ai-01 is not `none` [inferred].
- Visual sample: a realistic AI persona beside a distinct agent mark, both labelled [S-L19-111] [inferred pairing].
impact now / as it grows:
- Distinct mark: now, the AI is recognizable at once. As it grows, more agents join the same shape family and none is mistaken for a colleague [inferred].
- Faceless or cartoon: now, cheap to make. As it grows, in one app neither earned users' trust [S-L19-111].
- Realistic persona: now, a helper that feels trustworthy for personal advice [S-L19-111]. As it grows, it needs a consistent portrait set, voice and label, and people may credit it with more ability than it has (DC-L13-16) [inferred].
standards: STD-visual-details-36 (the same look means the same behavior, so an AI drawn exactly like a person would be read as one [inferred]), STD-visual-details-45 (anticipate misuse and harm in AI features).

title: Whether images change for each person
questions: (questions the designer answers) Do the images stay the same for everyone, or change with what each person has told the product? Based on what: their goals, a trait they chose, or their own photo? On which screens?
options:
- **The same images for everyone.** Today's implicit default; no source argues for it directly [inferred].
- **Images that reflect the person's goals or identity.** After the paywall's design, personalization moves the numbers most: calling out the person's name, highlighting their goals, and an image that represents their identity (in a fitness app, a strong man for a male user) [S-L19-106] (one paywall designer's ranking).
- **An avatar from a trait the person chose.** Personalizing the avatar by zodiac sign made Moonly feel more personal [S-L19-111].
- **The person's own face in product images.** Moonly put each user's face into around 50 images in the product: complex and expensive to build, the results were inconsistent and some were simply cringe, thousands of users avoided opening the app, and the feature was removed. People are sensitive to anything involving their own face [S-L19-111].
visual effect: Goal-matched images make a paywall feel made for the person [S-L19-106]; a chosen-trait avatar feels personal [S-L19-111]; the person's own face, rendered unevenly, feels embarrassing enough to keep people away [S-L19-111].
depends on: what onboarding asks (DC-L19-129), the imagery subject and photo brief (DC-L19-72, Q-img-01), who pays (DC-L19-75), the paywall pattern (DC-L19-135), which personal data the product may use (STD-visual-details-41).
affects: paywall and onboarding images, avatars (DC-L19-76), the image asset manifest (one set per goal plus a default), and the tests that compare them.
token encoding: None (a content decision). The builder keeps image sets keyed by the stated answer, such as `assets/paywall/<goal>.jpg`, with a default set [inferred names].
platform notes: None from the sources.
accessibility constraints: Each variant has its own alt text (DC-L05-14) [inferred]. Pick the variant from what the person said about their goals, not from a guessed trait, and keep the whole range of people across the sets (DC-L05-14's inclusion rule; STD-visual-details-43, design for every age and ability) [inferred]; the source's gendered example stays an example, not a rule.
default: (default + heuristic) The same images for everyone, with a default set always present. When onboarding already asks about goals, one image set per stated goal on the paywall and onboarding is worth testing, once the screen's design itself has been tested [S-L19-106]; an avatar may use a trait the person chose [S-L19-111]. Never generate product images from the person's own face [S-L19-111] (one app; STD-visual-details-41, ask for private data only when needed, and STD-visual-details-45, cut a feature whose risk outweighs its value, point the same way [inferred]).
maps to:
- New question Q-img-10 (stage 18, zoom 3; show if Q-aud-02 is `consumer` or `play` [inferred]): "Should some images change with what each person tells you, like their goals?" Options `same-for-all` (default), `by-stated-goal` ("image sets matched to the goal people chose in onboarding, tested on the paywall") [S-L19-106], `chosen-trait-avatar` ("an avatar from something they picked, such as a zodiac sign") [S-L19-111]; `own-face` listed as not recommended, with Moonly's result as the reason [S-L19-111].
- Q-img-01 hook: with `by-stated-goal`, ask for one image set per goal plus a default [inferred].
impact now / as it grows:
- Same for everyone: now, one image set to make. As it grows, the easiest to keep consistent, at the cost of feeling less personal [inferred].
- By stated goal: now, a paywall that speaks to each person [S-L19-106]. As it grows, every new goal multiplies the image sets and the tests [inferred].
- Chosen-trait avatar: now, a personal touch at little cost [S-L19-111]. As it grows, each new trait needs its own artwork [inferred].
- Own face: now, a striking idea. As it grows, costly, uneven and off-putting; Moonly removed it [S-L19-111].
standards: STD-visual-details-41, STD-visual-details-43, STD-visual-details-45.

title: Which interactions get no motion (the frequency gate)
questions: (questions the designer answers) Which things will people use all day, and should those move at all? Which actions start from the keyboard? Where is motion allowed to take its time?
options:
- **Gate by how often it is seen (house standard).** Four tiers decide before any curve is picked [S-L19-018] [S-L19-023] [S-L19-024] [S-L19-033]:
- 100+ times a day (keyboard shortcuts, command palette toggle, core navigation; on iOS and Android also tab switches, keyboard open and close, scrolling and settings toggles): no animation; on native, the platform default or nothing [S-L19-016].
- Tens of times a day (hover effects, list navigation, frequent toggles, press feedback, row selection): near-imperceptible or none; in React Native under 150ms [S-L19-016].
- Occasional (modals, drawers, sheets, toasts, settings, onboarding steps): standard motion.
- Rare or first-time (onboarding, first run, empty states, success, celebration): the delight budget (DC-L19-83).
- Real example: Raycast opens with no animation at all, which the author calls the optimal experience for something opened hundreds of times a day [S-L19-012].
- **Purpose-only test (practitioner videos).** Animate only when motion adds clarity or functionality and remove animation that does nothing [S-L19-054]; motion should support clarity, not distract [S-L19-084]. No video uses frequency as a test [inferred], so on its own this lets frequent surfaces keep motion.
- **Animate a little everywhere.** Small hover interactions on almost everything keep a simple site from feeling bland [S-L19-063], and buttons should almost always get a small animation [S-L19-054]. The hover tip comes from a portfolio and marketing-site context [S-L19-063]; the button tip is stated as a general rule that "context matters" qualifies [S-L19-054]. Inside product UI both break STD-when-to-animate-07, except for press feedback, which both sides endorse (DC-L19-93) [inferred].
- **OpenDesigner today.** No question or default says what stays still (recorded as a conflict under STD-when-to-animate-01). Differs from DC-L06-10 and the Q-motion-01 use/avoid line, which give expressive motion to page transitions and the primary action, both high-frequency surfaces [inferred].
visual effect: Gated: tools people use all day feel instant and wired to their hands, and the few things that do move stand out. Ungated: motion delights at first, then becomes annoying and makes the interface feel slower [S-L19-012] [S-L19-003]. An arrow-key list highlight that animates visibly lags behind the key presses [S-L19-012].
depends on: Q-scope-06 (operate or persuade), Q-plat-03 (keyboard input), Q-aud-02 (stakes), the component inventory (Q-comp-01 and stage 20).
affects: every component's motion spec; command palette, menus, tabs, list rows and hover states; the DESIGN.md Motion section, which should say what never moves; review severity (animation on a keyboard or high-frequency action is a HIGH finding [S-L19-027]).
token encoding: none (process decision). Record the tier per component in the component spec, for example `$extensions: {"opendesigner.motion": {"frequency": "100+/day", "animate": false}}` [inferred].
platform notes: iOS and Android keep tab switches, keyboard open and close, scrolling and settings toggles at the platform default or instant; Expo Router tabs use `animation: 'none'` [S-L19-016]. On the web, keyboard-initiated actions (shortcuts, focus jumps, arrow-key list highlight) never animate [S-L19-018] [S-L19-023] [S-L19-024] [S-L19-012].
accessibility constraints: Removing motion never removes feedback: a keyboard action still shows an immediate state change. The macOS video accepts a state change as the minimum ("micro animations, or at least a state change") [S-L19-067], but its own shortcut-opened quick-save panel slides in, slides away and collapses into a toast, which STD-when-to-animate-06 does not allow; only its state-change minimum carries over. Visible focus stays. Reduced motion is a separate layer (DC-L19-92).
default: (default + heuristic) Gate on. Tier every component in the inventory; ship no animation on 100+/day and keyboard-initiated actions; expect to reject most motion ideas (at most 5-7 suggestions for a whole app [S-L19-024]). Rule of thumb: the more often it is seen, the less it moves; when unsure, delete the animation [S-L19-032].
maps to:
- New question Q-motion-11 (proposed, zoom 2, first among the stage's zoom-2 questions; below zoom 2 the gate applies silently with the default tiers, since Q-motion-01 is asked at zoom 1): "Which things will people use all day? Those will not move." Show the inventory pre-sorted into the four tiers so the person only corrects which component sits in which tier; default: the tiers above. The answer can move a component between tiers but cannot give motion to a 100+/day or keyboard-initiated action, which the locked standards forbid (STD-when-to-animate-05, STD-when-to-animate-06) [inferred].
- Q-motion-01 use/avoid: replace "use expressive motion for page transitions, the primary action and alerts" with "no motion on things used all day or started from the keyboard; expressive motion only at rare moments (DC-L19-83)". Still open on 2026-09-28: the option notes now say that things done 100+ times a day get no animation, but the use/avoid line is unchanged (the conflict stays recorded under STD-when-to-animate-05).
- Visual sample: a command menu opened with and without animation, and arrow-key navigation with and without an animated highlight [S-L19-012].
impact now / as it grows:
- Gate by frequency: now, fewer animations to build and review, and the app feels fast. As it grows, each new component gets its tier at birth, so motion does not creep onto high-frequency surfaces and review can flag it [inferred].
- Purpose-only: now, fine for marketing pages. As it grows, frequent surfaces pile up motion that people meet hundreds of times a day, and the fix later is deletion [inferred].
- Animate everywhere: now, a lively demo. As it grows, a slower-feeling product and a larger reduced-motion surface to maintain [inferred].
standards: STD-when-to-animate-01, STD-when-to-animate-03, STD-when-to-animate-04, STD-when-to-animate-05, STD-when-to-animate-06, STD-when-to-animate-07, STD-when-to-animate-08, STD-when-to-animate-13, STD-when-to-animate-14, STD-when-to-animate-15, STD-when-to-animate-16, STD-when-to-animate-17, STD-when-to-animate-20.

title: Motion personality (amount and character)
questions: (questions the designer answers) Should motion feel crisp and quick, calm and elegant, or playful and bouncy? How much should move overall? May one component be livelier than the rest?
options:
- **Crisp and fast.** Fewer, subtler, fast animations; the house example is a professional dashboard [S-L19-023] [S-L19-024]. Kole: dashboard motion is "pretty tame and user focused" and people want a snappy, fast dashboard [S-L19-047]; his "snappy and performant" tone [S-L19-035].
- **Elegant.** Slightly slower than typical UI and using `ease` rather than ease-out, as Sonner's toast does (400ms ease) [S-L19-023] [S-L19-033] [S-L19-017]; Kole's "slow and smooth" tone [S-L19-035]. The house names elegance for one component, the toast, not for a whole product, so as a product personality it is [inferred]: only components whose own personality calls for it enter on `ease`, and every other entrance stays on ease-out (STD-easing-duration-01).
- **Playful.** More motion and bouncier springs for a playful consumer app [S-L19-023] [S-L19-024]; Kole's "fun and springy" tone [S-L19-035]. Bounce still comes only after a gesture that carried momentum or at a deliberately playful, rare moment, within 0.1-0.3 (DC-L19-88).
- **Polish as a consumer differentiator (practitioner, 2026-09-28).** In Mobbin's paywall video, paywall designer Jonathan Parra says animations "work really well" and expects the consumer apps that invest in animation, custom characters and world building (Focus Town) to win, now that anyone can ship an app; the host adds that polish can be why someone picks one product over another [S-L19-104]. Mobbin's onboarding study praises long consumer onboarding flows carried by animation (a lovable raccoon in Bipul, as auto-captioned; animated loading and verification in Bump) [S-L19-107]. Two videos from one channel, about consumer subscription apps; the same paywall video also tells of an ugly, text-heavy paywall that beat every design Parra tried for one app, and concludes there is no universal best paywall, only better experiments [S-L19-104]. Both place the polish in onboarding, characters and paywalls, which are rare or first-time moments, not everyday controls [inferred].
- **Minimal.** Only feedback and state changes move: press scale and short opacity fades. It replaces today's `none` option, GOV.UK's no-motion posture (DC-L09-06); under the house standards "minimal" cannot mean zero, because press feedback (STD-mobile-touch-05, a must) and state-explaining fades stay [inferred from STD-mobile-touch-05 and STD-accessibility-motion-02].
- **Two-mode (current default).** Plain for most actions, bold for 1-3 key moments per flow (Carbon, Material) [DC-L04-19]. Differs from the house rule: bold moments belong to rare or first-time moments, not to every flow, page transitions or the primary action (STD-when-to-animate-09).
- **Springs throughout (current option).** Differs from STD-springs-gestures-01: motion that no finger drives runs on a timing curve. Its useful part (springs for touch) moves to DC-L19-87.
visual effect: Crisp reads competent, fast and quiet. Elegant reads calm and refined. Playful reads alive and physical. Minimal reads still but responsive. The curve itself sets the tone [S-L19-035]. One bouncy component in a crisp app reads as a defect and is a review finding [S-L19-025] [S-L19-032].
depends on: Q-brand-01 sliders, Q-brand-04 (liveliness), Q-aud-02 (high-trust caps it), Q-scope-06, DC-L19-81.
affects: which component recipes differ from the plain set (the toast's ease, DC-L19-99), how many delight moments exist (DC-L19-83), bounce on momentum settles (DC-L19-88), the show-if of Q-motion-04 and Q-motion-06, and the levers `energy` dial.
token encoding: a string token `motion.personality` = `crisp | elegant | playful | minimal` that selects component recipes within the locked budgets [inferred]. Durations stay `$type: duration` and curves `$type: cubicBezier`; there is no DTCG type for personality.
platform notes: Native screen transitions keep the platform default whatever the personality [S-L19-016].
accessibility constraints: Personality never overrides reduced motion (DC-L19-92), the 300ms UI budget or the 1s ceiling; bounce disappears under reduced motion.
default: (default + heuristic) Default by audience: `playful` when Q-aud-02 is `play`; `crisp` in every other case, including Q-scope-06 `operate` and Q-aud-02 `work` (today's defaults) and `consumer`; Q-aud-02 `high-trust` always caps at `crisp`, as today's cap does at `productive`; `elegant` is offered to anyone but never chosen by default [inferred]. The Mobbin polish argument does not move the `consumer` default: a consumer product that wants to compete on polish keeps `crisp` everyday motion and spends the polish in named delight moments (DC-L19-83), which is where both Mobbin videos put it [S-L19-104] [S-L19-107] [inferred]. Rule of thumb: personality changes how many things move and a component's curve within the job rules, never the budgets. Differs from DC-L04-19 and DC-L09-06, whose defaults use "ease-in exit" and "springs only for spatial moves in the expressive mode": exits use ease-out (DC-L19-85) and springs follow the finger in every mode (DC-L19-87). The levers `energy` dial should stop swapping curve families and stretching durations past the budgets (conflicts recorded under STD-easing-duration-02 and STD-easing-duration-07) [inferred].
maps to:
- Q-motion-01: new option `crisp` replacing `productive` (drop the Carbon curve `cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0.38, 0.9)`, which is not a house curve); new option `elegant`; `springs` renamed `playful` with bounce only after momentum; `none` renamed `minimal` (press feedback and fades stay); `two-mode` retired, its "few big moments" moving to DC-L19-83. Partly done on 2026-09-28: `none` is now labelled "Minimal motion" and keeps press feedback and fades, `productive` is labelled "Quick, plain curves", and `springs` is marked as breaking STD-springs-gestures-01. Still open: `productive` still cites the Carbon curve, there is no `elegant` option, and `two-mode` is still the default. The `none` label promises that press feedback and fades stay, but engine.py still maps `none` to `raw.flags.motionOff`, which sets the feedback, enter, exit and expand transitions to 0ms in every context, so the generated tokens keep neither (checked in engine.py on 2026-09-28; not yet recorded in standards.json, and it falls short of the 100-160ms press in STD-mobile-touch-05).
- Q-motion-01: new default `crisp` (`playful` only for Q-aud-02 `play`, as above) because daily use argues for less motion [S-L19-024]. The default text already says "ease-out to enter and to exit" (done); it still says "springs only for spatial moves in the expressive mode", which should become "springs wherever a finger drives the motion" (STD-springs-gestures-01).
- Q-motion-01 `playful` option note (new heuristic): "for consumer apps, polish (characters, animated onboarding, a celebrated milestone) goes into rare moments, not into everyday motion" [S-L19-104] [S-L19-107] [inferred].
- Visual sample: one dropdown and one toast played in each personality: crisp (dropdown 200ms ease-out), elegant (toast 400ms ease), playful (a flicked card settling with bounce 0.2).
impact now / as it grows:
- Crisp: now, fast and cheap to build. As it grows, stays consistent as components are added; the risk is a flat feel, answered by a few rare delight moments.
- Elegant: now, a calm, premium feel. As it grows, every new component needs the slower `ease` recipe checked against the 300ms rule and a stated reason.
- Playful: now, a lively brand. As it grows, more motion to review and more reduced-motion variants; bounce must stay tied to gestures or it spreads to everyday controls.
- Polish in crisp plus delight moments: now, a calm product with a few crafted peaks (an animated first run, a character, a milestone). As it grows, the peaks are isolated pieces that can be redone without touching everyday components [inferred].
- Minimal: now, almost nothing to maintain. As it grows, feedback gaps appear unless press and state changes are kept.

title: Where the delight budget goes (rare moments)
questions: (questions the designer answers) Which rare moments may show off a little? Is there a first run, a milestone or an empty screen worth celebrating? In a product people come back to every day, what is celebrated every day and what only at a milestone? Is any of this motion there to grab attention rather than to answer the person?
options:
- **No delight moments.** Everything uses standard motion. For tools people open with a clear goal, the house removes friction instead of adding delight (STD-when-to-animate-20).
- **Onboarding and first run.** Kole calls onboarding the best time for mobile users to be captivated (Craft: a clean screen, a swipe, then tools sliding up from the bottom) [S-L19-084]; an onboarding step that wraps into the next slide in the swipe's direction [S-L19-035]. Mobbin's study of 1,460 onboarding flows adds real examples: Runkeeper's animation on first open shows what the app does before you read a word, and Bipul (name as auto-captioned) carries a 61-screen flow with a lovable raccoon you get to name [S-L19-107]. House: explanation motion is allowed only on marketing and onboarding surfaces (STD-when-to-animate-10), so an explaining first-open animation fits.
- **Waiting steps inside a long first-run flow (practitioner).** Bump animates even its loading and verification states, so something is always happening and the long flow does not feel boring [S-L19-107] (one video). The house gives onboarding steps standard motion, not delight (STD-when-to-animate-08), so this carries over as state indication paced by the wait (DC-L19-95), not as a celebration on every step [inferred].
- **Success and completion.** A check mark that slides in through a mask instead of fading [S-L19-059]; toasts with celebratory success messages and particles [S-L19-079].
- **Milestones in a daily routine (practitioner).** Streak milestones collected like badges (Opal) [S-L19-105]. Mobbin's streak video says that once a streak is routine the reward becomes predictable and loses its pull, so apps keep adding surprise animations, milestone celebrations and bonus XP; the same video warns that this optimizes engagement, not lasting habits [S-L19-105]. That agrees with the house reason for keeping delight rare, that delight seen daily fades [S-L19-012] [inferred link]; the house answer is not to manufacture surprise but to celebrate only the milestone (a 7-day or 30-day mark) and give the everyday completion standard confirmation [inferred]. DC-L19-136 owns the streak mechanic itself.
- **Empty states and error pages.** Kole: a 404 page is the ultimate time to be quirky [S-L19-063]; empty states are in the house rare tier [S-L19-024].
- **Rarely used components.** A morphing feedback button is delightful only because people use it rarely [S-L19-012].
- **Attention motion on offers (practitioner).** Mobbin's paywall video pairs a one-time offer with animation and haptic feedback to pull attention at the moment of upgrading [S-L19-104]; Focus Flight shapes its one-time offer as a flight ticket that prints while the phone vibrates [S-L19-107]. A one-off offer passes the frequency gate (it is rare), but its motion still needs a purpose the house accepts (STD-when-to-animate-03): a standard entrance, or delight in its own right, as the onboarding study calls Focus Flight's ticket [S-L19-107]; motion added to pull attention to the upgrade, which is how the paywall video describes it, names no such purpose [inferred]. The haptic differs from STD-springs-gestures-61, which keeps haptics for success, error, commit and snap and never fires one on an entrance the person did not cause (DC-L19-98) [inferred reading].
- **Rejected: motion that fakes chance.** A predetermined spin-the-wheel Lottie file that lands on a discount works for weekly revenue, but Parra says he has a hard time accepting it, and the video warns that when every app uses fake urgency people stop believing it [S-L19-104]. A wheel with a fixed outcome presents a fixed discount as luck, the kind of trick DC-L13-15's deceptive-pattern policy covers (fake urgency, fake scarcity) [inferred mapping], and none of the house's valid purposes for motion fits it (STD-when-to-animate-03) [inferred].
- **Current: 1-3 key moments per flow, including opening a page or the primary action** (DC-L04-19, DC-L06-03 via Q-brand-04 `hero-moments`). Differs: page opens and primary actions recur far more often than the rare tier allows (conflict recorded under STD-when-to-animate-09).
visual effect: Kept rare, delight lands as a pleasant surprise; used daily it fades and slows people down [S-L19-012]. The streak video reaches the same point from the reward side: a predictable reward loses its pull [S-L19-105]. Animated waiting steps make a long first-run flow feel shorter [S-L19-107]. Attention haptics and fixed-outcome wheels trade trust for a short-term lift; people learn to close paywalls because an offer follows [S-L19-104].
depends on: DC-L19-81, DC-L19-82, Q-pattern-04 (onboarding style; DC-L19-129 proposes splitting it into a separate onboarding question), Q-brand-04, the progress or streak mechanic (DC-L19-136), paywalls and offers (DC-L19-135).
affects: onboarding screens and the first-open animation, empty states, success states, success toasts, milestone and badge components, the 404 page, offer and paywall screens, and the haptics and sound at these moments (DC-L19-98); Lottie is used only for illustration and celebration, never UI state [S-L19-016].
token encoding: none (process decision). The chosen moments can be recorded as a string list in `$extensions` (`opendesigner.motion.delightMoments`) [inferred]; DC-L19-130 proposes `$extensions.builder.delightMoments` for the same list, and only one key should exist [inferred].
platform notes: React Native uses Lottie or Skia for illustration and celebration [S-L19-016]. On phones a milestone may get one success haptic, fired on the moment itself (STD-mobile-touch-62, STD-springs-gestures-59).
accessibility constraints: Each delight animation ships with its reduced-motion version in the same change, including character animations and a printing ticket (STD-accessibility-motion-01). The house bans slow loops near 0.2 Hz. Kole adds a pause and play button to a shimmer [S-L19-079] (single video), but his reason is that its uneven speed may bother some people, not accessibility; a stop control for looping decoration is only [inferred] from it. No haptic on an entrance the user did not cause, and a haptic is never the only signal (STD-accessibility-motion-20).
default: (default + heuristic) Pick a few named rare moments (1-3 [inferred]; no source gives a count): first run and milestones by default, plus first-use empty states and the 404 page where the product has them; never a component people use daily. In a product with a daily routine, the daily completion gets standard confirmation and the celebration waits for the milestone [inferred from S-L19-105 and STD-when-to-animate-09]; an everyday work tool gets no surprise motion to keep it "engaging" (STD-when-to-animate-20). Motion on a one-off offer may be a standard entrance or a designed delight moment, never motion added to pull attention; an attention haptic and anything that fakes chance are out. Rules of thumb: if a person meets it more than occasionally, it is not a delight moment; if it is there to grab attention rather than to answer the person, it is not delight either [inferred]. Changed on 2026-09-28 from "first run and success" to "first run and milestones", because the streak video shows that routine successes lose their pull [S-L19-105], and to match DC-L19-130's default.
maps to:
- Proposed Q-motion-12 (zoom 2, show if Q-brand-04 is `hero-moments` or `expressive`, so it does not re-ask what Q-brand-04 decided): "Which rare moments should get a little celebration?" It is the same question as DC-L19-130's proposed Q-pattern-10 (zoom 3, same show-if), so it should be asked once. This card now uses DC-L19-130's options (`first-run`, `first-empty`, `milestone`, `not-found`, `none`) and its default (`first-run` and `milestone`), replacing its own earlier default "first run and success", and proposes that the single question sit in stage 16 at zoom 2 as Q-motion-12, with Q-pattern-10 dropped; if the patterns lane keeps Q-pattern-10, drop Q-motion-12 instead [inferred].
- Same question, option note on `milestone` (new heuristic): "the milestone is celebrated; the everyday completion is only confirmed" [S-L19-105] [inferred].
- Q-brand-04 option `hero-moments`: reword "expressive motion and type only at significant moments such as opening a page or the primary action" to "at rare moments such as first run, milestones and empty states". Partly done on 2026-09-28: its now and grows notes already say "a first success" and "first run or finishing a task"; the option's label still names opening a page and the primary action.
- Offer haptics and the lesson sound: see DC-L19-98 (Q-motion-09, Q-motion-08).
- Visual samples: a success check sliding in through a mask after a spinner [S-L19-059]; onboarding tools sliding up from the bottom [S-L19-084]; a first-open animation that shows what the app does without text (Runkeeper) [S-L19-107]; streak milestones collected as badges (Opal) [S-L19-105]; a daily completion confirmed quietly next to a 30-day milestone celebrated [inferred pairing].
impact now / as it grows:
- None: now, nothing extra to build. As it grows, the product can feel generic; adding moments later is easy because they are isolated.
- Onboarding and first run: now, a strong first impression. As it grows, onboarding changes with features, so the motion must be cheap to rebuild.
- Animated waiting steps: now, a long first-run flow feels shorter. As it grows, every new step or check needs motion, so reuse one loading recipe [inferred].
- Success, empty states and 404: now, small, contained work. As it grows, each new flow asks for its own success moment; keep a shared recipe so they stay consistent [inferred].
- Milestones in a routine: now, the everyday loop stays quick and the milestone stands out. As it grows, rewards and milestones pile up; keep them tied to the person's own goal rather than to engagement for its own sake [S-L19-105] (DC-L19-136).
- Attention motion and haptics on offers: now, may lift a conversion. As it grows, people learn to expect and close offers [S-L19-104], and every attention haptic teaches them to ignore vibration [inferred].

title: How lively the marketing pages may be
questions: (questions the designer answers) Does the marketing site get more motion than the app? How much: none, a few moving parts, polished details, or scroll storytelling?
options:
- **No effects.** Calm and fast; the conversion-focused sites Kole shows, such as linear.app with dark mode and some glass but no heavy animation [S-L19-040].
- **A few moving parts.** huddle.works's minimal motion [S-L19-040]; simple, tasteful hover effects (Welcome, Pipe, Klaviyo) instead of heavy graphics [S-L19-066]; photos slightly zooming in or out and staggered slide-ups [S-L19-085]; one well-built hover animation that demonstrates the product (Intercom) [S-L19-084].
- **Polished details.** Kole's "level four": a blur on the multi-select, a mega menu that stays open and slides its content instead of closing and reopening, a call to action that appears on hover only when needed [S-L19-072]; an explanatory animation in the first viewport (Linear's Product Intelligence) [S-L19-012].
- **Scroll storytelling and 3D.** Prometheus Fuels-style scrollytelling for awareness sites: memorable but heavy [S-L19-040]; scroll-driven process diagrams [S-L19-050]; parallax on elements in spacious margins [S-L19-063].
- **Load sequences (values from single videos).** A loading screen held 1,000ms then slid away over 800ms on a custom exponential curve [S-L19-081]; GSAP `expo.inOut` over 1.3s with a 0.2s stagger [S-L19-071]. These are marketing motion; the house allows longer, illustrative motion there. Three limits still apply: the same GSAP video grows its navbar from scale 0, which STD-enter-exit-origin-01 forbids on every surface; the loader leaving and the header text arriving are an exit and an entrance, which take ease-out rather than `expo.inOut` (STD-easing-duration-01, DC-L19-85) [inferred]; and Kole himself says to keep preloaders short because people are impatient [S-L19-069].
visual effect: From calm and fast to memorable but heavy. Kole's warnings: effects that slow loading or make navigating harder are probably not worth it [S-L19-040]; big or flashy animation overwhelms people [S-L19-069]; an imported scroll effect that renders blurry looks cheap (Coda) [S-L19-066].
depends on: Q-scope-01 includes `marketing`; Q-brand-05 (how marketing relates to the product); Q-scope-06 (`persuade` or `experience`); DC-L19-82.
affects: heroes, scroll reveals, logo marquees, navigation and mega menus, feature sections, 404; the performance budget (DC-L19-96).
token encoding: a separate marketing motion set beside the product set, for example `motion.marketing.reveal` = `$type: transition` {600ms, 0ms, [0.77, 0, 0.175, 1]} and `motion.marketing.image-reveal` {1000ms, same curve}, the house scroll and image reveal recipes [S-L19-017] [S-L19-010]; the product set is unchanged [inferred structure]. The standards already create the primitive `motion.duration.reveal` = 600ms (STD-enter-exit-origin-26) on the ease-in-out curve `motion.easing.standard` = [0.77, 0, 0.175, 1] (STD-easing-duration-02), so the marketing transitions should reference those rather than repeat the values [inferred].
platform notes: Web only in these sources. Mouse-following effects need a backup on tablets and phones [S-L19-069]; hover effects sit behind the fine-pointer gate.
accessibility constraints: Reduced motion removes parallax and scroll-driven movement. Marquee text reduces usability [S-L19-085] and loops should be slow enough to read [S-L19-069]. Scrolljacking "very sparingly, if ever" [S-L19-054] (single video, opinion). No full-viewport moving backgrounds and no slow 0.2 Hz loops (house). The two loop rules pull in opposite directions (slow enough to read, but not near one cycle per 5 seconds); the house rule wins [inferred].
default: (default + heuristic) Default `few-moving-parts` for conversion sites (Q-scope-06 `persuade`); `scroll-story` only for awareness or experience sites. Rules of thumb: the layout should look good before any animation is added [S-L19-082]; motion should point at the product [S-L19-084]; repeat one or two motion themes rather than one-off effects [S-L19-062] (Kole's view across videos, practitioner opinion). Scroll reveals fire once, 100px into view.
evidence: [S-L19-010] [S-L19-012] [S-L19-017] [S-L19-040] [S-L19-050] [S-L19-054] [S-L19-062] [S-L19-063] [S-L19-066] [S-L19-069] [S-L19-071] [S-L19-072] [S-L19-081] [S-L19-082] [S-L19-084] [S-L19-085]; compared with DC-L06-01 (via Q-brand-05) and DC-L19-133, which covers the same decision from the marketing-page side and agrees on `few-moving-parts`. Steve Schoger's landing-page build (S-L19-103, listed under Sources used as read and not cited) adds no motion guidance.
maps to:
- New question Q-motion-13 (proposed, zoom 2, show if Q-scope-01 includes `marketing`): "How lively should the marketing site be: still, a few moving parts, polished details, or scroll storytelling?" Default `few-moving-parts`. DC-L19-133 supports this question and adds its heuristic, "is this page built to convert or to be remembered?" [S-L19-040], so the marketing motion budget is asked once.
- Q-scope-01 option `marketing`: add that this is where longer, explanatory and scroll-triggered motion is allowed and where product-UI budgets relax.
- Visual sample: a mega menu closing and reopening versus staying open and sliding its content [S-L19-072]; the four levels as four hero strips.
impact now / as it grows:
- None: now, fastest to ship. As it grows, the site may feel flat against competitors; motion can be added section by section later.
- Few moving parts: now, modest build effort. As it grows, easy to keep consistent if the moving parts are shared recipes.
- Polished details: now, noticeably more build and QA time. As it grows, each new section must meet the same bar or the site looks uneven [inferred].
- Scroll storytelling: now, a memorable but heavy page. As it grows, costly to change copy or structure, and performance and reduced-motion work grows with every section [inferred].

title: Easing curves grouped by job
questions: (questions the designer answers) Which curve does each kind of movement use? Are curves grouped by job, by strength or by mood? Is ease-in ever allowed?
visual effect: Ease-out starts fast, so the interface feels responsive; two 300ms dropdowns side by side show ease-in feeling slower [S-L19-003]. Custom curves feel more energetic than CSS's built-in keywords [S-L19-003]. The drawer curve feels like an iOS sheet [S-L19-005].
depends on: DC-L19-82 (only a component with an elegant personality, such as the toast, enters on `ease`); DC-L19-87.
affects: every transition token; `motion.easing.exit` is removed; the engine's `motion.transition.enter`, `.exit`, `.move` and `.feedback` pick curves by job; the `motion.html` presets.
token encoding: `$type: cubicBezier`: `motion.easing.out` = [0.23, 1, 0.32, 1], `motion.easing.in-out` = [0.77, 0, 0.175, 1], `motion.easing.drawer` = [0.32, 0.72, 0, 1], `motion.easing.hover` = [0.25, 0.1, 0.25, 1] (CSS `ease`) [inferred equivalence], `motion.easing.linear` = [0, 0, 1, 1]. As built by the standards on 2026-09-28: `motion.easing.enter` and `motion.easing.exit` both hold [0.23, 1, 0.32, 1], `motion.easing.standard` holds [0.77, 0, 0.175, 1], and `motion.easing.drawer`, `motion.easing.hover`, `motion.easing.toast` and `motion.easing.linear` exist (STD-easing-duration-01, STD-easing-duration-02, STD-enter-exit-origin-41, STD-components-toasts-drawers-07).
platform notes: React Native uses the same beziers (`EASE_OUT`, `EASE_IN_OUT`, `EASE_SHEET`) and never Reanimated's built-in curves [S-L19-016]. Native screen transitions keep the platform's own curve.
accessibility constraints: none directly; the reduced-motion cross-fade uses 200ms `ease` (DC-L19-92).
default: (default + heuristic) The job-based set above. Ask: is it entering or leaving, moving on screen, a hover or color change, or constant? If none fits, use ease-out. Differs from DC-L04-21 and DC-L04-24, which give exits an accelerate curve.
maps to:
- Q-motion-03: new default "by job: ease-out (0.23, 1, 0.32, 1) to enter and leave, ease-in-out (0.77, 0, 0.175, 1) to move, `ease` for hover and color, linear for constant motion, drawer (0.32, 0.72, 0, 1) for sheets; no ease-in", because the house bans ease-in on UI and fixes one curve per job. Option `role-based` reworded to these four jobs; `intensity-based` and `personality-based` kept only as labels for comparison. Done on 2026-09-28: Q-motion-03's default is this set, it cites this card, and it is settled by STD-easing-duration-01 and STD-easing-duration-02 (not asked); the other two options are marked as breaking those standards. Confirms current default.
- Q-motion-01 default text: "ease-in to exit" becomes "ease-out to enter and exit". Done on 2026-09-28.
- Still open: the built tokens name the ease-out curve twice, `motion.easing.enter` and `motion.easing.exit` (both [0.23, 1, 0.32, 1]), and call the ease-in-out curve `motion.easing.standard` (STD-easing-duration-02); DC-L19-183 proposes the job names (`--ease-out`, `--ease-in-out`, `--ease-drawer`) as the exported aliases.
- Visual sample: two 300ms "Options" dropdowns, ease-in against ease-out, with the curve graph; built-in against custom ease-in-out [S-L19-003].
impact now / as it grows:
- By job: now, five named curves and one question per animation. As it grows, new components pick a curve without debate, and review can check the job automatically [inferred].
- Role-based with an accelerate exit: now, familiar from Material and Carbon. As it grows, every exit feels sluggish and each becomes a review finding.
- By mood: now, expressive range. As it grows, curves drift between components and teams.
standards: STD-easing-duration-01, STD-easing-duration-02, STD-easing-duration-03, STD-easing-duration-13, STD-easing-duration-17, STD-components-toasts-drawers-40, STD-enter-exit-origin-39.

title: Duration budget per element
questions: (questions the designer answers) How long does each kind of element take to appear? Do things leave faster than they arrive? What may take longer than 300ms?
options:
- **A budget per element (house).** [S-L19-018] [S-L19-017] [S-L19-016] [S-L19-015]
- web: button press 100-160ms (recipe 160ms); tooltips and small popovers 125-200ms (recipe 125ms); dropdowns and selects 150-250ms (recipe 200ms); modals 200-500ms (recipe 250ms); drawers 500ms on the drawer curve; toasts 400ms `ease` (Sonner's personality);
- iOS and Android: press 100-150ms (recipe 120ms); toggles, chips and small state changes 150-200ms; sheets, modals and drawers a spring of about 300ms perceived; screen transitions at the platform default (iOS push 350ms);
- UI stays under 300ms unless a reason is stated; nothing runs over 1s unless it is illustrative [S-L19-001]; a 180ms select or dropdown feels more responsive than a 400ms one [S-L19-003] [S-L19-012]; exits about 20% faster (the React Native toast: 300ms in, 250ms out) [S-L19-015] [S-L19-004], although the web recipes run dropdowns, tooltips and modals at the same duration both ways [S-L19-017]; larger elements and longer travel get longer [S-L19-004].
- **Six-step ladder (current Q-motion-02 default, DC-L04-20).** Instant 0, micro 100, short 150-200, medium 250-300, long 400-500, extra 700. Differs: `long` and `extra` pass the UI budget with no named reason, and there is no 125ms tooltip step.
- **Four semantic steps (Primer) or 16 steps (Material 3)** [DC-L04-20].
- **Energy-scaled ladder (levers `motion.durationMultiplier` 0.8-1.2).** Differs: it stretches menus and modals past their budgets.
- **Marketing lengths (single videos).** 800ms slides after a 1,000ms hold [S-L19-081]; 1.3s moves [S-L19-071]. Allowed only as illustrative marketing motion (DC-L19-84).
visual effect: Short durations feel connected to the click; long ones feel sluggish. Faster exits get out of the way and respect people's time.
depends on: DC-L19-81, DC-L19-82, DC-L19-85; the component inventory; platform (Q-plat-01).
affects: every duration token and component recipe; engine `validate` thresholds (an advisory above 300ms, not above 400ms and 500ms); `motion.duration.long` and `extra` for UI.
token encoding: `$type: duration`: `motion.duration.press` 160ms, `motion.duration.tooltip` 125ms, `motion.duration.dropdown` 200ms, `motion.duration.modal` 250ms, `motion.duration.drawer` 500ms, `motion.duration.toast` 400ms (as built by the standards on 2026-09-28: `tooltip` 125ms, `modal` 250ms, `drawer` 500ms and `toast` 400ms exist, the ladder is now `micro` 100, `short` 150, `medium` 200 and `long` 250ms, and press uses `micro` 100ms, all within the budgets; STD-easing-duration-07, STD-enter-exit-origin-09, STD-enter-exit-origin-11, STD-enter-exit-origin-41, STD-components-toasts-drawers-07); exit tokens derived at 0.8 of the stored entrance value so they follow a locked value, applied where a recipe has a separate exit (the web popover, tooltip and modal recipes share one duration for both directions, so they keep it) [inferred]; the 300ms budget stored as a validation rule in `$extensions` [inferred].
platform notes: React Native keeps tens-per-day motion under 150ms and press feedback at 100-150ms [S-L19-016], with 120ms and a 3% scale as the press recipe's ceiling [S-L19-015]; native screen transitions are never overridden.
accessibility constraints: Motion that runs by itself for more than 5 seconds needs pause, stop or hide (WCAG 2.2.2, cited in DC-L04-20) [inferred]; the 1s ceiling holds.
default: (default + heuristic) The per-element budget. Rule of thumb: if it is UI and over 300ms, name the reason (a drawer, a toast's personality) or cut it to 150-250ms. Differs from DC-L04-20 (steps up to 700ms, exits 20-35% shorter).
maps to:
- Q-motion-02: new option `per-element` (the table above) as the new default, because the house times each element within its own budget; `6-steps` loses `extra 700` and keeps `long` for drawers only; `asymmetric` becomes part of the default at about 20% (not 20-35%). Partly done on 2026-09-28: Q-motion-02 is settled by STD-easing-duration-07 and STD-easing-duration-11 (not asked), and `6-steps` and `16-steps` are marked as breaking STD-easing-duration-06 and -07. Still open: the stored default still reads "6 steps; exits about 70-80% of the entrance ... never blocks input longer than about 100ms", which contradicts its own settling standards and STD-springs-gestures-13; it should read "per-element budget, exits about 20% faster, never blocks input".
- Visual sample: the 180ms and 400ms selects opened one after the other [S-L19-003]; a timeline showing each element's band.
impact now / as it grows:
- Per element: now, more named tokens (about six). As it grows, each new component inherits a band and stays fast; the budget doubles as a review check [inferred].
- Six-step ladder: now, fewer tokens. As it grows, components reach for `long` and `extra`, and the product slows down.
- Energy-scaled: now, one dial feels powerful. As it grows, a small dial change silently moves every duration past its budget.
standards: STD-easing-duration-06, STD-easing-duration-07, STD-easing-duration-09, STD-easing-duration-10, STD-easing-duration-11, STD-easing-duration-12, STD-easing-duration-13, STD-enter-exit-origin-08, STD-enter-exit-origin-09, STD-enter-exit-origin-11, STD-enter-exit-origin-41, STD-components-toasts-drawers-07, STD-components-toasts-drawers-08, STD-mobile-touch-05, STD-mobile-touch-42.

title: What drives each motion: timing curve, spring or keyframes
block path: Foundations > Motion > Motion driver and interruptibility
questions: (questions the designer answers) Which motion follows a finger and needs springs? Can people grab or reverse something while it moves? Can they keep working while things animate?
options:
- **Springs for anything a finger drives, timing for everything else (house).** Drags, flicks, swipes and anything a finger can interrupt settle on a spring with the release velocity; motion no finger started runs on a curve and a duration [S-L19-016] [S-L19-018] [S-L19-020]. Springs carry their velocity through an interruption [S-L19-019].
- **CSS transitions for things triggered rapidly.** Stacking toasts, toggles, expand and collapse retarget from where they are; keyframes restart and jump (Sonner's keyframes-versus-transitions demo) [S-L19-006] [S-L19-018].
- **Keyframes or CSS animations for predetermined motion** that nobody interrupts; they run off the main thread and stay smooth while the page is busy [S-L19-023] [S-L19-033].
- **Springs throughout** (current Q-motion-01 `springs`; Apple and M3 Expressive in DC-L04-19 and DC-L04-22). Differs: the house keeps plain on-screen moves on ease-in-out timing.
- **Duration and easing only** (Carbon, Fluent, Polaris, Primer in DC-L04-22). Differs: it cannot serve drag-driven UI.
- **Blocking input briefly.** DC-L04-24 allows input to be blocked for up to about 100ms [inferred in that card]. Differs: the house never locks input, not even during a stagger.
visual effect: Springs feel continuous and grab-able; timing feels predictable; keyframes on rapid UI make elements jump; blocked input feels broken.
depends on: Q-plat-03 (touch), Q-plat-08 (stack), DC-L19-82.
affects: sheets, drawers, carousels, toasts, toggles, accordions, card stacks; the engine's `motion.transition.move`, which today points plain on-screen moves at a spatial spring (conflict under STD-springs-gestures-01).
token encoding: timing motion as `$type: transition` {duration, delay, timingFunction}; springs as a number group in `$extensions` (DC-L19-88); each motion token states which driver it uses [inferred].
platform notes:
- Web: walk down CSS transition, `@starting-style`, CSS animation, WAAPI, then Motion (springs, layout, exit and gesture values) and stop at the first that fits [S-L19-018]. A spring pre-sampled into CSS `linear()` is a fixed-duration curve and cannot take a release velocity (conflict recorded under STD-springs-gestures-16) [inferred].
- React Native: Reanimated CSS transitions for state changes; a shared value with `Gesture.Pan()` for anything a finger touches [S-L19-016].
- SwiftUI: start the animation in the synchronous callback, on the event's frame [S-L19-034].
accessibility constraints: Never block input during a transition. Under reduced motion, springs become cross-fades (DC-L19-92).
default: (default + heuristic) Use a spring if a finger was involved and timing for everything else [S-L19-016]. The web house sources add two more spring cases: decorative mouse-tracking values go through a spring (`useSpring`, STD-springs-gestures-45), and so may an element meant to feel alive, such as a Dynamic Island-style morph [S-L19-018] [S-L19-023]. Anything that can fire twice in a second uses transitions, not keyframes. Nothing locks input.
maps to:
- Q-motion-04 show-if: from "Q-motion-01 is two-mode or springs" to "Q-plat-03 includes `touch`, or the product has any drag or swipe (DC-L19-97)", because springs follow the finger, not the personality. Since 2026-09-28 Q-motion-04 is settled by STD-springs-gestures-02 and -04 and is not asked, so the show-if only matters if a person overrides those standards; it is still worth correcting so the question's text does not tie springs to a personality.
- Q-motion-02 default text: "never blocks input longer than about 100ms" becomes "never blocks input". Still open (see DC-L19-86).
- Q-motion-01: option `springs` reworded as described in DC-L19-82.
- Visual sample: toasts added quickly with keyframes against transitions [S-L19-006]; a sheet grabbed while it closes and following the finger.
impact now / as it grows:
- Springs for touch, timing elsewhere: now, a JS spring library only where gestures exist. As it grows, new gesture components reuse the same spring presets and stay interruptible.
- Springs throughout: now, one model. As it grows, a JS dependency on every surface and plain moves that overshoot.
- Timing only: now, cheapest. As it grows, adding a draggable sheet later means introducing springs anyway.
standards: STD-springs-gestures-01, STD-springs-gestures-12, STD-springs-gestures-13, STD-springs-gestures-14, STD-springs-gestures-15, STD-springs-gestures-16, STD-springs-gestures-45, STD-performance-properties-13, STD-performance-properties-15, STD-swift-45.

title: Spring parameters and presets
questions: (questions the designer answers) How should springs be described: bounce and duration, damping and response, or physics numbers? How much bounce is allowed, and when? Which presets exist?
options:
- **Damping ratio and response (Apple's designer parameters; house).** Default settle 1.0 with a response of 0.3-0.4s (move or reposition 1.0 / 0.4); about 0.8 only after a flick; sheet or drawer 0.8 / 0.3; rotation 0.8 / 0.4; a dismissal that must stop at a hard edge stays at 1.0 with overshoot clamping [S-L19-020] [S-L19-015] [S-L19-016]. Motion mapping: `{ type: 'spring', bounce: 0, duration: 0.4 }`, and bounce 0.2 after a flick [S-L19-020]; the web drag settle recipe is `{ duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.2 }` [S-L19-017]. Reanimated: `{ duration: 400, dampingRatio: 1 }` and so on [S-L19-016].
- **Duration and bounce (current Q-motion-04 `apple-bounce`: 0, 0.15, 0.3).** Close; differs in that the house recommends 0.2 and allows 0.1-0.3, and only after momentum or at playful moments [S-L19-033].
- **Mass, stiffness and damping.** `{ mass: 1, stiffness: 100, damping: 10 }` when more control is needed [S-L19-018] [S-L19-033]. Kole's Figma springs are in this form: a hover name tag at 500ms, stiffness 636, damping 24 [S-L19-079] and a spinner at stiffness 550, damping 40 [S-L19-059] (single-video values). With mass 1 the name tag works out to a damping ratio of about 0.48 [inferred], a visible bounce on a pop-up with no gesture behind it. The house's own physics example (mass 1, stiffness 100, damping 10) works out the same way to 0.5 [inferred], and the same stiffness and damping drive its decorative mouse-tracking example [S-L19-023], so STD-springs-gestures-05 permits this much bounce only as a deliberately playful or decorative moment, never on an everyday pop-up [inferred].
- **Material spatial and effects springs with energy-driven damping (current DC-L04-22 default and levers).** Stores damping ratio and stiffness; lets spatial hero motion overshoot, and the `energy` dial under-damps every spatial spring above 33. Differs: overshoot only after momentum.
visual effect: Damping 1.0 settles smoothly with no overshoot; 0.8 overshoots slightly, like a thrown object; about 0.5 bounces visibly and reads as gimmicky on everyday UI [inferred].
depends on: DC-L19-87; DC-L19-82 (playful may use the top of 0.1-0.3).
affects: `motion.spring.*` tokens; sheets, drawers, carousels, picture-in-picture style moves, rotating elements.
token encoding: DTCG has no spring type (DC-L04-22). Store the designer parameters as a number group in `$extensions`: `motion.spring.settle` {dampingRatio 1.0, response 0.4}, `motion.spring.momentum` {0.8, 0.4}, `motion.spring.sheet` {0.8, 0.3}, `motion.spring.rotate` {0.8, 0.4}, `motion.spring.dismiss` {1.0, 0.3, clamp true}; derive stiffness for Compose and bounce for SwiftUI and Motion at export [inferred]. As built by the standards on 2026-09-28: `motion.spring.momentum`, `motion.spring.sheet` and `motion.spring.rotation` are transition tokens whose `$extensions.opendesigner.spring` holds {dampingRatio, stiffness, mass 1}, with stiffness derived from the response (0.4s gives 246.7, 0.3s gives 438.6), and the spatial spring is overridden to damping ratio 1.0 and stiffness 246.7 (STD-springs-gestures-04, -06, -08, -09). The values match this card; the stored pair differs, since STD-springs-gestures-02 asks for damping ratio and response, which DC-L19-190 also recommends storing, with stiffness derived at export. No clamped dismiss token exists yet.
platform notes: Reanimated takes `duration` and `dampingRatio`, never mass, stiffness and damping [S-L19-016]; Motion takes bounce and duration [S-L19-020]; Compose needs stiffness, derived at export [inferred].
accessibility constraints: Reduced motion drops springs and overshoot in favour of a cross-fade.
default: (default + heuristic) Four presets plus a clamped dismiss, as above. Rule of thumb: bounce only when a finger threw it; nothing that appears on its own overshoots. Differs from DC-L04-22 (stiffness stored, energy-driven damping, under-damped hero moves) and from Q-motion-04's 0.15 step.
maps to:
- Q-motion-04: new default "damping ratio and response, four presets (settle 1.0/0.4, momentum 0.8/0.4, sheet 0.8/0.3, rotate 0.8/0.4) plus a clamped dismiss", because these are the values Apple ships and the house locks. Partly done on 2026-09-28: Q-motion-04 is settled by STD-springs-gestures-02 and -04 (not asked), and all three options are marked as breaking a standard. Still open: the stored default still reads "(dampingRatio, stiffness) plus derived (duration, bounce) ... pre-sampled `linear()` for CSS", which contradicts STD-springs-gestures-02 (designer parameters) and STD-springs-gestures-16 (a sampled `linear()` cannot take a release velocity).
- Q-motion-04 option `apple-bounce`: values become 0 and 0.2 (range 0.1-0.3). Option `spatial-effects`: add "moves never overshoot unless a gesture carried momentum". Both are now marked as breaking standards, so this only matters if a person overrides one.
- Visual sample: one drag released three ways, 1.0, 0.8 and about 0.5, with the release velocity carried in [S-L19-020]; a sheet dismissed with a clamped spring beside one snapping back.
impact now / as it grows:
- Damping and response presets: now, five named springs. As it grows, every new gesture reuses a preset and exports cleanly to each platform.
- Duration and bounce: now, easy to read. As it grows, fine if the bounce range stays 0.1-0.3.
- Physics numbers: now, maximum control. As it grows, hard to review; teams drift into bouncy values [inferred].
- Energy-driven damping: now, one dial. As it grows, raising energy makes every plain move bounce.
standards: STD-springs-gestures-02, STD-springs-gestures-04, STD-springs-gestures-05, STD-springs-gestures-06, STD-springs-gestures-07, STD-springs-gestures-08, STD-springs-gestures-09, STD-springs-gestures-10, STD-springs-gestures-45, STD-mobile-touch-51, STD-accessibility-motion-02.

title: How things appear and leave
questions: (questions the designer answers) Do menus and popups grow out of the button that opened them? Do things only fade, or also scale or slide a little? Do they leave the way they came?
options:
- **Scale and fade from the trigger (house recipes).** Dropdowns, popovers, menus and selects: opacity 0 plus scale(0.95) from the trigger's transform origin, 200ms ease-out; tooltips scale(0.97), 125ms; modals centered, scale(0.96), 250ms, with the backdrop fading on the same timing [S-L19-017]. Never from scale(0), which looks like it comes out of nowhere; start at 0.9 or more, like a deflated balloon that still has a shape [S-L19-003] [S-L19-004]. Leave along the same path: a toast that enters from the bottom leaves through the bottom [S-L19-012].
- **A small slide plus fade (practitioner, Figma prototypes and a marketing page).** A hidden menu placed a couple of pixels lower so it slides up as it fades in [S-L19-059]; a hover name tag rising from slightly lower at opacity 0 [S-L19-079]; decorative marketing elements entering in a way that suits them (a star that rotates and pops, a balloon that flies in) [S-L19-063]. The menu and the name tag agree with the house rule that entrances carry a small transform [inferred]. The star and the balloon are decorative marketing entrances, where the house allows longer, illustrative motion (STD-easing-duration-06); a balloon flying in from off-screen is not a small transform, and a "pop" still starts at 0.9 or more, never scale(0) (STD-enter-exit-origin-01) [inferred].
- **Plain fade (current Q-motion-06 option `fade`: "Fade for in-screen enter and exit").** Differs: the house forbids opacity-only entrances except a modal's backdrop and the reduced-motion variant, and DC-L04-23 itself records Material's pattern as fade plus scale. Kole calls a plain fade-in "robotic" for decorative elements on a landing page [S-L19-063].
- **Slide by the element's own size** for toasts, drawers and sheets, written as a percentage such as translateY(100%) [S-L19-023] [S-L19-033].
- **Clip-path reveal** for images and reveals: inset(0 0 100% 0) to inset(0 0 0 0) on the ease-in-out curve, with no layout shift [S-L19-010].
visual effect: Scaling from the trigger makes the panel look like it came out of what was clicked; center-origin popovers look wrong, most of all at the top right [S-L19-003]. scale(0) pops from nothing; a plain fade looks flat.
depends on: DC-L19-85, DC-L19-86; the component primitives (Base UI and Radix expose the trigger origin as a CSS variable).
affects: popover, dropdown, menu, select, tooltip, modal and backdrop, toast, drawer, accordion (height and opacity 200ms), image reveals, and glass surfaces, which materialize by animating blur and scale together rather than fading (STD-enter-exit-origin-31).
token encoding: component recipe tokens, for example `popover.motion.enter` = `$type: transition` {200ms, 0ms, [0.23, 1, 0.32, 1]} with `popover.motion.from-scale` = `$type: number` 0.95; `tooltip.motion.from-scale` 0.97; `modal.motion.from-scale` 0.96 [values from S-L19-017; names inferred]. Transform origin is a CSS convention, not a token. As built by the standards on 2026-09-28, the starting scales already exist as primitives: `motion.scale.enter` 0.95, `motion.scale.enter-tooltip` 0.97 and `motion.scale.enter-modal` 0.96 (STD-enter-exit-origin-08, -09, -11); component recipes should reference them.
platform notes: React Native uses Reanimated layout animations (`entering`, `exiting`) and percentage translates for sheets [S-L19-016]; the web uses `@starting-style` with a mounted-flag fallback [S-L19-023].
accessibility constraints: Reduced motion keeps the opacity and drops the scale and slide (DC-L19-92).
default: (default + heuristic) The house recipe set. Rule of thumb: everything that enters gets opacity 0 plus a small transform; anything anchored to a trigger grows from it; modals grow from the center; everything leaves the way it came.
maps to:
- Q-motion-06 option `fade`: reword to "fade plus scale from the trigger for menus and popovers (0.95, 200ms), tooltips (0.97, 125ms), centered dialogs (0.96, 250ms)". Partly done on 2026-09-28: `fade` is now marked as breaking STD-enter-exit-origin-02, so it is never recommended; the reworded option that follows the standard does not exist yet.
- Visual sample: the "Options" element entering from scale(0) and from 0.93 [S-L19-003]; the feedback popover toggled between center and trigger origin [S-L19-003]; a menu sliding up a couple of pixels as it fades in [S-L19-059].
impact now / as it grows:
- Scale from the trigger: now, needs primitives that expose the origin. As it grows, every new anchored overlay looks connected to its trigger for free.
- Small slide plus fade: now, simple in Figma prototypes. As it grows, fine if the distance stays small and the path is the exit path.
- Plain fade: now, cheapest. As it grows, every overlay reads flat and each becomes a review finding.
standards: STD-enter-exit-origin-01, STD-enter-exit-origin-02, STD-enter-exit-origin-03, STD-enter-exit-origin-04, STD-enter-exit-origin-06, STD-enter-exit-origin-08, STD-enter-exit-origin-09, STD-enter-exit-origin-11, STD-enter-exit-origin-12, STD-enter-exit-origin-16, STD-enter-exit-origin-17, STD-enter-exit-origin-21, STD-enter-exit-origin-23, STD-enter-exit-origin-26, STD-enter-exit-origin-31, STD-enter-exit-origin-38.

title: Screen and page transitions
questions: (questions the designer answers) When people move between screens or tabs, does anything move? Who owns it on iOS and Android? Should an item grow into its own detail page?
options:
- **Platform-owned.** The native stack at the platform default (iOS push 350ms); a modal for a self-contained task people can abandon; a form sheet with detents for a short interruption; the back swipe mirrors any custom animation [S-L19-016] [S-L19-015]. Agrees with DC-L10-14 on screens; DC-L10-14's "shared brand motion for in-content micro-interactions (as springs)" differs, because springs are only for motion a finger drives (STD-springs-gestures-01).
- **No animation for tabs and core navigation.** Tab switches never slide or fade (Expo `animation: 'none'`) [S-L19-016]; core navigation is in the 100+ a day tier [S-L19-024].
- **Continuity (shared element, container transform).** A card that expands into a page, an image that zooms into the next page's hero, transitions that follow the swipe's direction [S-L19-035] (Kole calls the plain slide "lame": opinion); the vocabulary names shared-element, continuity and direction-aware transitions [S-L19-019]; a mega menu that stays open and slides its content [S-L19-072].
- **Direction carries meaning.** Sliding up from the bottom means temporary; a screen sliding in from the left shows progress, as in onboarding [S-L19-084] (single video; consistent with the shared-axis pattern in DC-L04-23 [inferred]).
- **Material's four patterns including fade-through for tabs (current Q-motion-06 default "all four plus stagger", DC-L04-23).** Differs: fade-through between tabs breaks STD-when-to-animate-14.
- **Custom swipe back with the background moving in from about 35%** [S-L19-053] (single-video number); relevant only to custom or web builds, since native back stays with the OS [inferred].
visual effect: Native transitions feel at home and keep the back gesture. Continuity keeps people oriented. Animated tabs feel slow when used all day.
depends on: DC-L19-81, Q-plat-01, Q-plat-08, Q-motion-09.
affects: router configuration, the tab bar, detail pages, onboarding flows, web view transitions.
token encoding: none for native screens (delegated to the OS). Web: one `motion.transition.navigate` transition for occasional drill-ins only [inferred]; tabs have none.
platform notes: Android predictive back and iOS swipe-back stay native (DC-L10-14). On the web, a view transition morphs between states and connects shared elements [S-L19-019].
accessibility constraints: Under reduced motion, native stacks switch to `animation: 'fade'` [S-L19-015] and spatial transitions become fades.
default: (default + heuristic) Platform default on native, configured through native stack options and never rebuilt in JavaScript; no animation on tab switches and core navigation; on the web, a continuity transition only for occasional drill-ins (card to detail) and onboarding, while on native the same idea stays inside one screen (a card expanding in place) [inferred]; forward moves sideways, temporary things come from the bottom [inferred from S-L19-084 and DC-L04-23].
maps to:
- Q-motion-06: new default "platform transitions for screens (native stack on iOS and Android), none for tabs and core navigation, container transform for occasional drill-ins on the web, shared axis x for onboarding; no fade-through between tabs", because tab switches are an all-day action and native screen transitions stay with the platform. Still open on 2026-09-28: `fade-through` is now marked as breaking STD-when-to-animate-05 and -14, but the default still reads "all four plus stagger", so the default includes an option the stage says never to recommend.
- Q-motion-09: keeps default `os-nav-brand-micro`, with its label "small brand springs inside content" reworded to "small brand micro-motion inside content, on springs only where a finger drives it" (STD-springs-gestures-01); DC-L19-98 adds the haptic map to the same default. Still open: the label is unchanged; the haptic part is done (see DC-L19-98).
- Visual sample: an image zooming into the next page's hero against a plain page slide [S-L19-035]; a mega menu closing and reopening against sliding [S-L19-072]; a tab switch that is instant.
impact now / as it grows:
- Platform-owned: now, nothing to build. As it grows, new OS behaviour (such as predictive back) arrives for free.
- None for tabs: now, instant. As it grows, stays fast as tabs are added.
- Continuity: now, extra build per drill-in. As it grows, each new detail page needs a matching shared element, so keep it to a few patterns [inferred].
- Fade-through for tabs: now, looks polished in a demo. As it grows, slows the most-used navigation.
standards: STD-when-to-animate-05, STD-when-to-animate-14, STD-mobile-touch-42, STD-mobile-touch-44, STD-accessibility-motion-04, STD-easing-duration-06, STD-springs-gestures-01.

title: Stagger for groups of items
questions: (questions the designer answers) When a group of items appears, do they come in one after another? How far apart? Which lists skip it?
options:
- **30-80ms per item, only for groups seen occasionally (house).** Web recipe: each item from opacity 0 and translateY(8px) over 300ms ease-out, delays 0, 50, 100 and 150ms [S-L19-017] [S-L19-033]; React Native: `FadeInDown.duration(250).delay(index * 40)` [S-L19-015]. Never blocks interaction; no entrance on lists people scroll past all day; never on rows of a virtualized list.
- **20-50ms per item, total at most 500ms (current Q-motion-06 option, DC-L04-23; Carbon 20ms).** Differs: 20-29ms is below the house floor and there is no condition on how often the list is seen.
- **Longer marketing staggers (single videos).** Navbar items 0.2s apart, 0.6s each [S-L19-071]; phone screens sliding up one after another on load [S-L19-085]. Marketing or illustrative motion, outside the UI range. A text highlight that sweeps across as the page scrolls [S-L19-069] is scroll-linked rather than a timed stagger [inferred].
- **Steps revealed as work progresses (practitioner, product UI).** An AI research trail whose three steps fade in one by one [S-L19-055] (no timing given). Each step shows real progress, so it is state indication paced by the work rather than a decorative stagger [inferred].
- **No stagger.** The group appears together.
visual effect: A short stagger reads as a natural cascade; a long one feels slow; an entrance on an all-day list gets in the way.
affects: lists, grids, search results, a dashboard's first load, onboarding.
token encoding: `motion.stagger.step` = `$type: duration` 50ms (40ms in React Native); `motion.stagger.item` = `$type: transition` {300ms, 0ms, [0.23, 1, 0.32, 1]} [values from S-L19-017 and S-L19-015; names inferred]. As built by the standards on 2026-09-28, the step exists as `motion.duration.stagger` = 50ms (STD-enter-exit-origin-13).
platform notes: React Native defines layout-animation builders at module scope or in `useMemo` [S-L19-016].
accessibility constraints: Under reduced motion the translate goes and the opacity stays, or the items appear together [inferred from STD-accessibility-motion-02]; input is never blocked.
