title: Where the delight budget is spent
block path: Foundations > Brand > Expression > Hero moments (by pattern)
questions: (questions the designer answers) Which moments get celebratory or playful treatment: the first run, first-use empty states, success after a real milestone, the 404 page? Which never do? How rich may a success message be?
options:
- **None:** calm everywhere. For tools people open with a clear goal, the house standard is to remove friction instead of adding delight (STD-when-to-animate-20).
- **Rare moments only:** first run, empty states, success or completion, and celebration are the only places where bounce, a generous stagger or a longer beat belong [S-L19-024]; this is STD-when-to-animate-09.
- **Candidate moments named by the sources:** a welcome page that sets the tone (the Motion Passport) [S-L19-007]; an onboarding surprise after a clean start (Craft) [S-L19-084]; an empty dashboard with an animation (Dub) [S-L19-044]; celebratory success toasts with particles [S-L19-079]; a success check that slides in through a mask instead of fading [S-L19-059]; milestone badges, such as saving 30 days in a row [S-L19-078]; a quirky 404 page with a quiz, a movie character or a mini game, the best place to be playful because the user doesn't belong there [S-L19-063]. New from Mobbin: a game in place of an empty table once every bill is paid (Mercury) and a birthday cake inside an ownership donut chart (Cake) [S-L19-110]; streak milestones collected like badges (Opal) [S-L19-105]; a founder's note at first run (DC-L19-37) [S-L19-107]; and polish (animation, custom characters, world building) forecast by a paywall consultant as what will set the most successful apps apart [S-L19-104].
- **Surprise to keep a routine engaging:** once a streak is routine, apps add surprise animations, milestone celebrations and bonus XP to keep the loop unpredictable [S-L19-105]. The same video warns this optimises engagement, not lasting habits; DC-L19-83 answers it by celebrating the milestone and only confirming the daily completion.
- **Attention motion on offers:** a one-time offer with animation and haptics [S-L19-104], a ticket-shaped offer that prints while the phone vibrates [S-L19-107]. DC-L19-83 allows the animation as a rare moment and rules out the attention haptic (STD-springs-gestures-61).
- **Everywhere:** delight on frequent actions. Ruled out: STD-when-to-animate-09 bans it on components people use many times a day, and STD-when-to-animate-05 bans any motion at 100+ uses a day.
visual effect: Delight kept for rare peaks makes them memorable, which matches the peak-end rule in the L13 research (design the ends, celebrate sparingly at real peaks), and keeps daily use fast [inferred link]. Delight on frequent actions feels slow and gimmicky (DC-L04-19).
depends on: how lively the brand is (Q-brand-04, DC-L06-03), motion style (Q-motion-01, DC-L04-19), the product's personality (STD-easing-duration-13), tone for success and errors (Q-voice-02, DC-L19-37).
affects: success states, toast variants, EmptyState, the 404 template, the welcome screen, milestone and badge components, sound and haptics (Q-motion-08, Q-motion-09).
token encoding: the expressive motion set already planned as a mode (DC-L04-19 `motion-scheme: expressive`); nothing new. The chosen moments are recorded once, under DC-L19-83's key (`$extensions` `opendesigner.motion.delightMoments`, for example `["first-run", "first-empty", "milestone", "not-found"]`, the option ids of the shared question) [inferred]; this card's earlier `$extensions.builder.delightMoments` is dropped so only one key exists, as DC-L19-83 asks.
platform notes: haptics and sound only for meaningful moments such as success, at most one haptic per action (STD-springs-gestures-61), and never as the only feedback (STD-accessibility-motion-20).
accessibility constraints: under reduced motion, celebrations keep a short cross-fade instead of movement (STD-accessibility-motion-02); particle bursts must not flash more than three times a second (WCAG 2.3.1) [inferred]; a playful 404 still says where you are and gives a way back (STD-visual-details-33, DC-L19-37).
default: (default + heuristic) Keep Q-brand-04's default `hero-moments` and name the moments: the welcome screen after sign-up, the first-use empty state, the completion of a rare and meaningful task (a first project published, a milestone), and the 404 page. Heuristic: ask how often this person will see it (STD-when-to-animate-04). Tens of times a day means no delight (a "copied" confirmation stays subtle, STD-when-to-animate-07); once, or at a milestone, means it is eligible. DC-L06-03 sets "one or two hero moments" and DC-L04-19 "1-3 hero moments per flow", but their examples (opening a page, the primary action) recur far more often than STD-when-to-animate-09 allows; DC-L19-83 records that conflict and rewords `hero-moments` to "at rare moments such as first run, milestones and empty states". This card follows DC-L19-83 and gives the interview a concrete list to offer. It differs from [S-L19-079], which suggests celebratory success toasts in general: under STD-when-to-animate-09 only rare successes qualify. Updated in this revision: the default moments are now first run and milestones (in a daily routine, the milestone is celebrated and the everyday completion only confirmed, which is DC-L19-83's answer to the streak video's warning that manufactured surprise serves engagement, not habits [S-L19-105] [inferred]), which is also DC-L19-83's default; a rare all-done state joins the eligible list [S-L19-110]; the consultant's view that polish sets apps apart [S-L19-104] is one practitioner's forecast, and under the house rules polish is spent on craft and rare moments, never on frequent actions (STD-when-to-animate-09, STD-when-to-animate-05).
maps to:
- Q-brand-04: keeps the default `hero-moments` with DC-L19-83's rewording. New follow-up: "Which moments get the lively treatment?" Multi-select `first-run`, `first-empty`, `milestone`, `not-found`, `none`; default `first-run` and `milestone` [inferred]. It is asked once, as DC-L19-83's proposed Q-motion-12 (stage 16, zoom 2, show if Q-brand-04 is `hero-moments` or `expressive`), which already uses these options and this default; this card's earlier Q-pattern-10 is withdrawn so the two cards make one change. Option note on `first-empty` (new): "includes a rare all-done state, such as every bill paid" [S-L19-110].
- Q-brand-04 visual samples: a plain success toast next to a celebratory one with particles [S-L19-079]; the 404 quiz and mini-game examples [S-L19-063]; Mercury's all-done game and Cake's donut chart [S-L19-110].
impact now / as it grows:
- *None:* now the fastest product. First runs and milestones pass without a moment people remember.
- *Rare moments only:* now a few crafted pieces. As features grow, the list stays short because frequency, not feature count, decides [inferred].
- *Everywhere:* now lively. Every frequent action pays the cost on every use, and it breaks the house standards.
- *Surprise to keep a routine engaging:* now keeps a daily loop fresh [S-L19-105]. As it grows, the surprises have to keep coming, and they serve engagement rather than the person's goal [S-L19-105] [inferred for "keep coming"].
standards: STD-when-to-animate-03, STD-when-to-animate-04, STD-when-to-animate-05, STD-when-to-animate-07, STD-when-to-animate-09, STD-when-to-animate-20, STD-easing-duration-13, STD-springs-gestures-61, STD-accessibility-motion-02, STD-accessibility-motion-20, STD-visual-details-47, STD-process-review-taste-67

title: Marketing visuals: show the real product
questions: (questions the designer answers) What fills the hero and the feature sections: stock photos, generic icons, a generated mock interface, a full screenshot, cropped views, or visuals made from the product for the page? How are screenshots captured and framed?
options:
(the "levels" of [S-L19-072], with the other sources placed on them)
- **Level one, unrelated imagery:** stock images that have little to do with the product undermine the whole page [S-L19-072]; generic feature icons read as vibe-coded [S-L19-061]; a fake interface an AI tool guessed from the app's description [S-L19-103].
- **Level two, the full product screenshot:** a big improvement and a source of color, but not framed, so it draws attention to nothing in particular [S-L19-072]. A real screenshot is a simple way to add a graphic when there are no other graphics; capture it at 3x, and match the site's grays and corner radius to the screenshot's [S-L19-103].
- **Level three, zoomed crops:** zoom in on the important parts to curate exactly what the viewer sees [S-L19-072]; in feature cards, crop the full screenshot to the feature being described, with the relevant state showing, such as a chart tooltip [S-L19-103].
- **Level four, visuals crafted for the page:** show exactly what the product does and let its color thread through the page [S-L19-072]; skewed link cards and lightly edited images of the product's own screens [S-L19-061].
- **Product-led motion:** the hero image slides and fades into the product view as the page scrolls, so the first thing motion shows is the product [S-L19-084]; the product's own "thinking" loader as a hero accent [S-L19-082]. (How much motion: DC-L19-133.)
- **Audience imagery:** images of the people and settings the product serves. A restaurant-software site with no images at all feels robotic, so its redesign uses moody restaurant photos to relate to its users [S-L19-062]. For a physical product such as a skincare brand, product photos on bright white with lots of space [S-L19-049].
visual effect: Product imagery makes the page read as a software company at first glance [S-L19-084] and meets the quality bar that builds trust [S-L19-061]. Stock images and generic icons make the page look like a template [S-L19-072] [S-L19-061]. Crops focus attention; crafted visuals feel made for the page [S-L19-072].
depends on: what the screens are for (Q-scope-06 `persuade`), whether marketing is in scope (Q-scope-01), photography (Q-img-01), whether a product UI exists to capture, where color comes from (DC-L19-01 `imagery-led`).
affects: hero, feature sections, bento tiles, social-proof sections, the screenshot capture step in the builder, open-graph images [inferred].
token encoding: no new tokens; the screenshot frame reuses radius and border roles (the see-through ring is DC-L19-09's decision). Capture scale as builder metadata, `$extensions.builder.screenshot.scale = 3` [inferred].
platform notes: web marketing pages. Capturing at 3x keeps screenshots sharp on high-density screens [S-L19-103] [inferred reason beyond "high resolution"].
accessibility constraints: each product image has alt text that says what it shows [inferred]; text that matters is real text on the page, not only pixels inside a screenshot (WCAG 1.4.5) [inferred]; text laid over imagery still meets 4.5:1.
default: (default + heuristic) For a software product with a marketing page: use the real product. A cropped or crafted product view in the hero, a cropped screenshot per feature, site grays matched to the product. Audience imagery may sit beside the product views where the page says who it is for [S-L19-062]; images unrelated to the product or its users never [S-L19-072]. Four videos agree on showing the product (three by Kole Jain [S-L19-061] [S-L19-072] [S-L19-084], one by Steve Schoger [S-L19-103]); no research card covers product imagery on marketing pages [checked L05 cards DC-L05-14 to DC-L05-21]. The nearest is DC-L05-20, where Atlassian's in-product onboarding illustrations use low-fidelity gray shapes and never real screenshots; that rule is for a different surface (inside the product), so the two do not conflict [inferred]. DC-L19-72 reaches the same default from the imagery side. OpenDesigner guardrail: the imagery is the person's own product; a reference site's screenshots are never reused (AGENTS.md "references give structure, never identity").
maps to:
- Q-img-01: supports DC-L19-72's new option `product-ui` ("real screenshots of your product, captured at 3x and cropped to each feature") and its default `product-ui` when Q-scope-01 includes marketing (today the default is `none`). This card adds one trigger: Q-scope-06 `persuade` with a product UI to capture. It is distinct from the existing `still-life` option, which covers photos of physical products.
- Q-img-01 visual sample: the four levels of one SaaS landing page side by side, from stock photo to crafted product visual [S-L19-072].
impact now / as it grows:
- *Stock or icons:* now quick. It never shows what the product does, and it ages with the stock library.
- *Full screenshot:* now honest and colorful. Every UI change makes the page out of date [inferred].
- *Crops:* now focused. Crops of small areas survive more UI changes than full screenshots [inferred].
- *Crafted visuals:* now the most work. Each new feature needs its own visual, but the page stays coherent [inferred].
standards: STD-when-to-animate-10, STD-process-review-taste-40, STD-visual-details-30

title: Calls to action on marketing pages
block path: Patterns > Marketing page > Call to action
questions: (questions the designer answers) How many main actions does the hero have? Is the first action a button, or a field people type into? Do the nav button and the hero button share a label? Where does the page ask again?
options:
- **One primary action:** one call to action and one main focus in the header, as Google and Apple do, because people are easily distracted; the same video allows "one or maybe two" things to look at and click [S-L19-040]; header sections get only one primary call to action, and if a second must stay, remove its fill [S-L19-057].
- **A primary and an unfilled secondary:** heading, subtext and a primary and secondary call to action [S-L19-049]; a hero with "Get started" and "Explore" used as a stagger exercise [S-L19-011]. These reconcile with the line above as one filled button plus one unfilled [inferred], which fits DC-L13-18's rule of at most one high-emphasis action per region.
- **Matching labels:** when the nav button and the hero button go to the same place, give them the same label, so people build the right mental model [S-L19-072].
- **A field as the call to action:** a search or prompt bar visitors can type into, which then sends them to log in; because they have already started acting, they are more likely to finish [S-L19-082]. Prompt products can drop the landing page and open on a large prompt box above the fold (ChatGPT, Gemini) [S-L19-055]. A "find a dealer" search bar instead of a button [S-L19-065]. Mobbin's onboarding review shows the same idea inside apps: letting people try the core experience before they sign up (Duolingo's first lesson; Elma, as auto-captioned), which it rarely sees in apps with AI features [S-L19-107]. That the web version works for the same reason is [inferred]; the app side is DC-L19-129's.
- **Asking again:** a call-to-action section is important when the header has none [S-L19-065]; the hero's typeable bar reused as the final call to action [S-L19-082].
- **Call to action on hover:** a level-four detail where a button appears on hover over the logo section, only when needed [S-L19-072]. Hover does not exist on touch.
visual effect: One filled button gives an obvious next step; two filled buttons draw equal attention and compete [S-L19-057]. A typeable field turns the hero into the product's first use [S-L19-082] [inferred for "first use"]. Matching labels read as one path [S-L19-072].
depends on: DC-L13-18 (one high-emphasis action per region), button styles (Q-state-01), hero axis (DC-L19-45), marketing copy (DC-L19-36), product type (a prompt or search product).
affects: the hero template, navigation, the final call-to-action section, button variants, an input-as-CTA component.
token encoding: none new; button emphasis tokens from DC-L13-18 (`button.primary.*`, `button.secondary.*`).
platform notes: web marketing. Hover reveals sit behind fine-pointer media queries (STD-accessibility-motion-15), so a hover-only call to action is missing on phones [inferred application].
accessibility constraints: a prompt or search field has a visible label or an accessible name, not a placeholder alone (the L13 placeholder-only warning); what the visitor typed survives the redirect to log in [inferred]; emphasis is carried by fill and shape, not color alone (DC-L13-18); targets meet 24 px.
default: (default + heuristic) One filled primary action per hero; any second action unfilled; the nav and hero buttons share a label when they share a destination; every long page ends with a call-to-action section, which is required when the hero has none. For prompt or search products, the input is the call to action. Never make a hover-revealed call to action the only way forward. This confirms DC-L13-18; "one primary" appears in two Kole Jain videos and in DC-L13-18, so it is treated as a rule rather than one creator's opinion.
evidence: [S-L19-040] [S-L19-057] [S-L19-049] [S-L19-011] [S-L19-072] [S-L19-082] [S-L19-055] [S-L19-065] [S-L19-107]. Compared against DC-L13-18, DC-L19-45, DC-L19-129 and DC-L19-104 (which adds, for Q-state-01, "strip the fill before adding a style" and a nav button one size smaller).
maps to:
- New question (proposed Q-pattern-08, zoom 2, stage 23, show if Q-scope-01 includes `marketing` or Q-scope-06 is `persuade`): "What should visitors do first: press a button, or start typing?" Options `button` (default), `prompt-field` (the visitor types a prompt or query) [S-L19-082] [S-L19-055], `search-field` (find a location or item) [S-L19-065].
- Q-state-01: confirms "one main button per area" for marketing heroes; new heuristic, "nav and hero buttons share a label when they share a destination" [S-L19-072].
- Visual samples: level one's mismatched nav and hero labels against level two's matching ones [S-L19-072]; a Gemini-style hero whose call to action is a typeable bar [S-L19-082].
impact now / as it grows:
- *One primary:* now a clear path. New campaigns compete for that one slot, which forces a choice [inferred].
- *Primary and unfilled secondary:* now covers two audiences. More secondary links creep in over time and need the same discipline.
- *Field as the call to action:* now engaging. It ties the landing page to the product's input and has to change when the product's input changes [inferred].
- *Final section:* now a second chance. It scales to long pages because each section can lead into it [inferred].
standards: STD-accessibility-motion-15, STD-visual-details-29, STD-visual-details-36, STD-mobile-touch-10

title: How much motion marketing pages get
questions: (questions the designer answers) Is the page built to convert or to be remembered? Does the marketing site get more motion than the product, and what is each effect for? Which effects are in: scroll reveals, preloaders, marquees, 3D, scrolljacking?
options:
- **Conversion first, few effects:** sites built to get people to buy or try (an invoicing site whose name the captions garble, Linear, Huddle) work without heavy effects; usability is at the heart of everything, and effects that slow loading or navigation are not worth it [S-L19-040].
- **Built to be remembered:** heavy scrollytelling (Prometheus Fuels) serves awareness, not purchase [S-L19-040]; a spinning 3D logo as the hero so the rest of the page needs little design [S-L19-046].
- **The maturity ladder:** no motion; simple load animations, which can feel cheap; smooth hover effects and fluid slider transitions; small high-quality details such as a blur transition or a mega menu that pushes content aside [S-L19-072]. Software sites are moving to simple, tasteful animation, and an imported scroll effect that renders blurry gives itself away [S-L19-066].
- **Motion with a job:** motion that draws attention to the product, such as a hero image sliding into the product view, or a single well-built hover animation that demonstrates the product; complex animation for its own sake makes navigation harder [S-L19-084]. An animation can replace a static asset when it explains a feature in the first viewport (Linear's Product Intelligence) [S-L19-012].
- **Specific effects:** preloaders add a premium feel and cover heavy media but must stay short [S-L19-069]; two build recipes hold the loader for 1,000 ms then slide it away over 800 ms [S-L19-081], or slide it over 1.3 s with `expo.inOut` [S-L19-071]; marquee text costs usability [S-L19-085]; scrolljacking rarely, if at all [S-L19-054]; scroll-revealed process diagrams and morphing media, keeping the changes small [S-L19-050].
visual effect: Pages with few effects can still be aesthetic, persuasive and usable; heavy effects are memorable but can load slower and make navigating harder [S-L19-040]. Level-four details signal quality [S-L19-072]. Motion that points at the product gives people an early first look at it [S-L19-084].
depends on: what the screens are for (Q-scope-06), how the marketing site relates to the product (Q-brand-05, DC-L06-01), how lively the brand is (Q-brand-04), motion style (Q-motion-01, DC-L04-19).
affects: hero entrance, section reveals, logo strip, preloader, product demo animations, mega menu, the marketing motion set.
token encoding: a marketing (expressive) motion set as a mode rather than duplicate tokens (DC-L04-19, DC-L06-01). Values from the standards: scroll reveal `clip-path` over `600ms` on the ease-in-out curve and image reveal `1s` `cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1)` (STD-easing-duration-09 values), as `duration` and `cubicBezier` tokens such as `motion.marketing.reveal.duration = 600ms` [inferred names]; group entrances stagger 30-80 ms per item (STD-enter-exit-origin-13).
platform notes: web marketing. Heroes use `min-height: 100svh` (STD-mobile-touch-10). Decorative mouse-tracking is allowed on marketing pages (STD-when-to-animate-11), but hover effects sit behind fine-pointer media queries (STD-accessibility-motion-15).
accessibility constraints: every effect ships with its reduced-motion version in the same change (STD-accessibility-motion-01, STD-accessibility-motion-02); no moving background behind the full viewport (STD-accessibility-motion-07); no slow loops near 0.2 Hz (STD-accessibility-motion-08); marquees and other auto-moving content over 5 s need a pause control (WCAG 2.2.2) [inferred]; a stagger never blocks input (STD-springs-gestures-13).
default: (default + heuristic) Default "convert" (DC-L19-84's `few-moving-parts`): motion that points at the product, scroll reveals that fire once on entry (STD-enter-exit-origin-27, STD-enter-exit-origin-28), one well-built signature interaction, no scrolljacking, and a preloader only when heavy media must load, kept short. Choose "remember" (`scroll-story`) only when the page's goal is awareness or Q-scope-06 is `experience`. Heuristic: first "is this page built to convert or to be remembered?" [S-L19-040], then "what does this effect point at?" (STD-when-to-animate-03). Marketing and explanatory motion may run past the 300 ms and 1 s caps (STD-easing-duration-06, STD-easing-duration-09), which covers the recipes' long preloaders, though STD-easing-duration-06 still asks whether a slow moment needs to be slow. Easing does not relax: entrances and exits ease out (STD-easing-duration-01), so the ease-in-out nav fade in [S-L19-081] and the `expo.inOut` slide that takes the loading screen off the page [S-L19-071] both use ease-out instead [inferred application]. The stagger follows STD-enter-exit-origin-13 (30-80 ms), which differs from DC-L04-23's 20-50 ms; the standard wins.
maps to:
- Proposed Q-motion-13 (DC-L19-84, zoom 2, show if Q-scope-01 includes `marketing`): supports its default `few-moving-parts` for pages built to convert and `scroll-story` only for awareness or experience sites. This card's "convert or remember?" [S-L19-040] becomes that question's heuristic rather than a separate question, so the marketing motion budget is asked once.
- Q-brand-05: confirms `one-system-two-sets`; the lively set is where marketing motion lives.
- Q-motion-01 visual sample: the same landing page at motion levels two, three and four [S-L19-072]; the hero image sliding into the product view [S-L19-084].
impact now / as it grows:
- *Convert:* now fast pages and less to build. As campaigns come and go, the few effects are easy to keep consistent [inferred].
- *Remember:* now memorable. Heavy effects take long to build and render and can slow loading [S-L19-040]; they are also costly to change and hard to keep accessible [inferred].
- *Motion with a job:* now each effect needs a reason. As features launch, the reason ("show the product") gives each new effect its brief [inferred].
standards: STD-when-to-animate-03, STD-when-to-animate-10, STD-when-to-animate-11, STD-enter-exit-origin-13, STD-enter-exit-origin-26, STD-enter-exit-origin-27, STD-enter-exit-origin-28, STD-easing-duration-01, STD-easing-duration-06, STD-easing-duration-09, STD-springs-gestures-13, STD-accessibility-motion-01, STD-accessibility-motion-02, STD-accessibility-motion-07, STD-accessibility-motion-08, STD-mobile-touch-10

title: Pricing pages and plan pickers
questions: (questions the designer answers) How many plans, on a web pricing page and on an in-app paywall? Which plan is selected or suggested first? What is biggest on a plan card, the name or the price? In which unit is the price shown, and where does the billed amount go? How are discounts, billing terms and plan differences shown? Where does Enterprise go?
options:
- **Fewer plans:** five plans (in an in-product billing tab) is not ideal; drop at least one, and rename a very high-volume plan to Enterprise because those customers probably need more than a fixed plan [S-L19-061]. Merge pages that sell the same thing into one plans section built on the few points that matter (for an AI product: cost, a better model, document uploads) [S-L19-082].
- **Two plans on an in-app paywall (new):** a yearly plan preselected, because it has the highest lifetime value (unless yearly does not suit the business), plus a weekly or monthly one; any other plans sit behind a "view all plans" button that opens a sheet, so the base paywall stays simple [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106]. Both videos are the same consultant, Jonathan Parra, so this is one voice. The sheet is DC-L19-114's decision.
- **How the paywall footer shows the price (new):** plan groups stacked or side by side, and both plans shown as a weekly amount with the real billed price as a subtitle, raised as things to test, not recommendations [S-L19-106].
- **Anchoring (new):** break the price into weekly amounts (Tide) or compare it with things people already pay for, such as coffee or therapy (Ahead) [S-L19-104]. A high-priced lifetime plan that is not meant to sell raises perceived value and nudges people toward the annual plan; 4% of iOS apps on Mobbin offer one, usually at about twice the annual price [S-L19-111]. Moonly kept the number and changed the unit (8 a month became 8 a week), because people compare prices with each other rather than with value; subscribers who converted at the weekly price churned harder [S-L19-111].
- **A plan recommended from the person's answers (new):** Grammarly recommends plans from its onboarding quiz and reports almost 20% more plan upgrades [S-L19-107].
- **Enterprise as a small link:** a tiny Enterprise button on every plan instead of its own section; the creator estimates it is irrelevant to about 98% of visitors [S-L19-082].
- **Card hierarchy:** plan name smaller and monthly price larger, because the price is what people care about [S-L19-061]. Give each plan a name and a short description, use check marks instead of bullets, list a feature the plan doesn't include, turn the button into an outline if it moves up the card, separate price and features with a light tint of the primary color instead of a divider, and write an actionable button label [S-L19-075].
- **Honest numbers:** show the actual discount, or discounted plans look cheaper than lower tiers and the order stops making sense; show what the next plan adds that the current one lacks (Resend, Supabase) [S-L19-061]; a note under the price with the real billing terms, so people don't feel misled when they learn what they will pay [S-L19-075]. A clearer offer can matter as much as a better one: Tipstop (as heard) emphasised its trial, added a discount badge and made the offer easier to understand, and reports direct conversions almost tripled with the same offer [S-L19-104].
- **One highlighted purchase:** the purchase call to action as one of the cards, marked with a gradient stroke [S-L19-082] (gradients are DC-L19-12's decision).
- **Billing inside the product:** tabs for billing and usage, usage as a few small donut charts, the billing email and payment method [S-L19-061].
visual effect: A larger price and a smaller name put the eye on what people decide by [S-L19-061]; check marks and a listed missing feature make plans easy to compare [S-L19-075] [inferred for "easy to compare"]; a clear discount keeps the order readable [S-L19-061]. The five-plan picker, with discounts that were not shown, looks like a mess [S-L19-061]. Two plans with one preselected lower the load of choosing [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106]. A weekly amount looks smaller than the same price per year [inferred], which is why the billed total must stay visible.
depends on: the deceptive-pattern policy (DC-L13-15: hidden costs, comparison prevention, preselection), one high-emphasis action per region (DC-L13-18), number styling (Q-type-06, DC-L19-33, which also carries the weekly-price footer sample), gradients (Q-color-25, DC-L19-12), the paywall screen (DC-L19-139), where the paywall appears (DC-L19-135).
affects: PricingCard, a plan comparison table, the paywall plan footer, the "view all plans" sheet, a plan badge, the billing settings page, upgrade prompts (DC-L19-135), a monthly or yearly switch.
token encoding: none new. Prices use tabular digits (STD-visual-details-02); a price that animates on a monthly or yearly switch uses NumberFlow (STD-visual-details-59) [inferred application]. The price-area tint is a `color` alias of the primary at reduced opacity, such as `color.pricing.price-area` [inferred name].
platform notes: Web pricing pages and in-product billing tabs come from Kole Jain's videos; in-app subscription paywalls on phones now come from Mobbin's [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106] [S-L19-111]. Apple began rejecting paywalls built on free-trial toggles in early 2026 [S-L19-104] (DC-L19-106 carries the rule for switches). Still not covered by any source: taxes, currencies, local prices, and monthly-or-yearly switches on web pages.
accessibility constraints: price and billing terms are real text at 4.5:1; a crossed-out old price also says it in words ("was $X"), because strikethrough is not announced reliably [inferred]; check marks and "not included" marks have text or accessible names, never an icon or color alone (WCAG 1.1.1, 1.4.1) [inferred]; the suggested or preselected plan is marked by more than color, such as a check or the word "Selected" [inferred]; the billed amount under a weekly price is body text, not faint fine print (DC-L19-36) [inferred].
default: (default + heuristic) Web pricing page: three or four plans, one of them suggested; the price larger than the name; the real discount and the billing terms under the price; what the next plan adds; Enterprise as a small link on each plan (still visible, so not hidden in the deceptive-pattern sense [inferred]). In-app paywall: two plans, the one that suits the business preselected (yearly, by the source's reasoning), the rest one tap away behind "view all plans" [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106]. Whatever unit is shown large, the billed amount and period are always on screen. The two surfaces differ, they do not contradict: all plans stay reachable, so the two-plan paywall is disclosure, not a cap, which respects the research warning that choice overload does not justify removing options (L13 law table) [inferred]. A preselected plan is a default choice, not the pre-ticked consent box DC-L13-15 flags, provided the other plan is as easy to pick [inferred]. A lifetime anchor is a real plan people can buy, so it may stay; a unit change is a price change and is shown plainly; neither may hide the billed total (DC-L13-15, hidden costs) [inferred]. No source settles where anchoring turns into misleading framing, so that stays a human review. Evidence strength: the plan count and the 98% figure are one creator's opinion; the three-to-four ceiling matches the L13 research's suggested info lint (a plan picker with more than 3-4 tiers and no suggested marker or comparison) [inferred there too]; the two-plan paywall and yearly default are one consultant's experience; Moonly's unit change and lifetime anchor are one app's results.
maps to:
- New question (proposed Q-pattern-11, zoom 3, stage 23, show if the product sells plans or Q-scope-06 is `persuade`): "How should your plans be shown?" Options `plan-cards` (3-4 cards, one suggested; default on the web), `comparison-table` (a feature grid when plans differ on many features) [inferred option], `single-plan` (one price plus an Enterprise link) [inferred option], and new `paywall-two-plans` ("Two plans, one preselected, the rest behind 'View all plans'"; default when plans are sold inside a phone app) [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106].
- Q-pattern-05: new detectable checks, "a discounted price shown without the real discount or the billing term" [inferred from S-L19-061 and S-L19-075] and "a price shown per week or per month with no billed amount and period on the same screen" [inferred from S-L19-106 and S-L19-111].
- Visual samples: a pricing card before and after (check marks, a listed missing feature, a billing note, a tinted price area, an outline button) [S-L19-075]; a vibe-coded plan picker fixed (fewer plans, smaller names, bigger prices, the real discount, the next plan's extras) [S-L19-061]; a two-plan paywall footer with yearly preselected, beside the weekly-price variant with the billed price as a subtitle [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106]; Tide's weekly breakdown and Ahead's comparison with coffee [S-L19-104].
impact now / as it grows:
- *Plan cards:* now easy to compare. As plans or features grow, cards overflow and a comparison table takes over [inferred].
- *Comparison table:* now thorough. It suits growing feature lists but reads as dense on phones [inferred].
- *Single plan:* now the simplest choice. As customer types diverge, it forces an early split into tiers [inferred].
- *Two-plan paywall:* now a quick choice. As plans are added, they go into the sheet, and the preselected plan has to be rechecked against the business [S-L19-106] [inferred].
- *Anchors and unit changes:* now may lift conversion. Moonly's weekly payers churned harder [S-L19-111], and every price change needs the honesty check again [inferred].
- *Honest numbers:* now a few more lines of text. They prevent support load and distrust as prices and discounts change [S-L19-075] [inferred for support load].
standards: STD-visual-details-02, STD-visual-details-59, STD-visual-details-29, STD-visual-details-31, STD-visual-details-35, STD-visual-details-44

title: Paywalls, upsells and re-engagement prompts
block path: Principles > Ethics > Monetization and engagement prompts
questions: (questions the designer answers) What may sit behind a paywall or an account wall? At which moments may a paywall or upgrade prompt appear, and is it one offer or one per feature? Can people close it? What happens when someone declines, tries to cancel or is about to leave? May the product comment on how much someone uses it, keep reminding them, or punish a lapse? Can people turn intrusive features off?
options:
- **Upgrade prompt at the limit:** show what the higher plan unlocks where the limit applies [inferred placement]; the source's hover version (after Dub) reveals the Pro limits by sliding the new limit in and the old number out, instead of crossed-out text [S-L19-079]; show what the next plan includes [S-L19-061].
- **Touch points across the customer's life (new):** after onboarding (the most used; 78% of iOS apps on Mobbin), at a gated feature, in settings, when a subscriber tries to cancel (a win-back offer) and before the app is deleted [S-L19-106] [S-L19-104]. A well-designed paywall at the wrong moment is still a bad paywall [S-L19-104].
- **One offer, or one paywall per feature (new):** every contextual, per-feature paywall lost Moonly's A/B tests, because people thought each feature had to be bought separately, so Moonly went back to one consistent paywall; the video then shows Orbit's paywall making clear that paying today unlocks all features [S-L19-111]. Parra says paywalls at different touch points speak more to the user because they are more personal [S-L19-104]. They fit as "many moments, one offer": show it where it is relevant, and each time say that one plan unlocks everything [inferred].
- **Soft or hard (new):** a soft paywall can be closed and the app used; Moonly's won across its tests, though its close button appears only after 5 seconds. A hard paywall has no way past without paying; the host reports that hard paywalls won in the US [S-L19-111].
- **Leaving and cancelling (new):** an exit-intent sheet that offers the monthly plan when someone turns down the yearly one [S-L19-104]; steep discounts kept for win-back when a subscriber tries to cancel, not straight after onboarding, where an 80%-off offer can cannibalise revenue [S-L19-106]; a longer trial instead of an aggressive last-minute discount, to stay compliant and keep trust [S-L19-104]. ClassPass takes fewer than five screens to subscribe and 17 to cancel [S-L19-104].
- **Offers that help (new):** Moonly's AI guide recommends an add-on only when that add-on can really help the person at that moment [S-L19-111]. In a demo whose brief asked where an offers nudge belongs without feeling manipulative, the agent put it on the home page right after onboarding, citing an app that does the same [S-L19-108].
- **A wall in front of simple content:** a recipe behind a paywall or an account requirement, presented as infuriating [S-L19-048].
- **Pressure tactics:** a usage-shaming message whose only choices are upgrading or more of the same notifications; a progress warning with a button nudging the user to lower their goal; a streak punishment that makes a reader guess where they were; endless pop-ups and premium tiers that add nothing [S-L19-048]. That video is satire: each is presented as what makes products maddening. New, from practice: a spin-the-wheel paywall whose wheel is predetermined to land on a discount, which the consultant says works for short-term weekly revenue while more and more people learn to close paywalls and wait for an offer [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106], and fake urgency, which the paywall video's narrator says people stop believing once every app uses it [S-L19-104]; a one-time offer that is gone once closed, paired with animation and haptics to pull attention [S-L19-104]; prices set by device (higher on a new phone on 5G), described without a word on fairness [S-L19-106].
- **An off switch:** three of the deliberately annoying features in the satire (the forced layer-naming modal, the streak punishment and neighbour control of smart-home devices) come with a way to turn them off: a notice, a button beside them or a setting [S-L19-048]. The usage-shaming message does not; its only choices are upgrading or more notifications.
- **The research policy:** DC-L13-15's enforced lint (pre-checked opt-ins, unequal accept and decline, re-prompting after a dismissal, fake countdowns, confirmshaming copy, cancelling harder than signing up).
visual effect: A prompt at the limit reads as help; a shaming or guilt prompt reads as hostile [S-L19-048]; a wall in front of simple content reads as a trap [S-L19-048] [inferred for "trap"]. One paywall that says it unlocks everything reads as one purchase; a string of per-feature paywalls reads as paying piece by piece [S-L19-111]. Fake urgency stops working once every app uses it [S-L19-104].
depends on: DC-L13-15 and Q-pattern-05 (still Planned), tone (DC-L19-37: never shame the user), pricing (DC-L19-134), the paywall screen (DC-L19-139), sheets (DC-L19-114), offer motion and haptics (DC-L19-83, DC-L19-98).
affects: upgrade banners and limit states, paywall screens, the exit-intent sheet, win-back and cancellation flows, the delete-account flow, one-time offers, notification and reminder prompts, streak and progress UI, feature toggles in settings.
token encoding: none; lint rules in `$extensions` or config (DC-L13-15).
platform notes: Apple began rejecting paywalls built on free-trial toggles in early 2026 [S-L19-104] (DC-L19-106). Moonly added Stripe beside Apple's payments in the US, partly because half of cancellations came within 3 minutes of purchase when cancelling was one tap, and reports lifetime value doubled; it advises against Google's alternative billing on Android [S-L19-111]. These are dated, market-specific reports. Where people pay (store, web or both) and what the store allows on a paywall are DC-L19-155's decision, which also proposes a Q-pattern-05 check for a free-trial toggle on an iOS paywall; this card does not repeat it. Notification permission primers are DC-L19-129's [S-L19-107].
accessibility constraints: an upgrade detail shown on hover also needs a non-hover path (STD-accessibility-motion-15) [inferred]; paywalls and prompts always have a way out (STD-accessibility-motion-24, STD-visual-details-33), visible from the first frame, so a close control delayed by 5 seconds [S-L19-111] does not qualify (DC-L19-114 says the same) [inferred application]; a decline option is never low-contrast (DC-L13-15 notes visual interference overlaps with contrast failures); a haptic fired when an offer appears is an entrance the person did not cause, which STD-springs-gestures-61 forbids (DC-L19-83, DC-L19-98) [inferred application].
default: (default + heuristic) Confirms Q-pattern-05's default `enforced`. Upgrade prompts appear at the limit, say what the next plan adds, and accept one dismissal that sticks (no re-prompting, the DSA example in DC-L13-15). Plan the paywall's moments (after onboarding, a gated feature, settings, cancel), but make every one the same offer that unlocks everything [S-L19-111] [S-L19-104] [inferred reconciliation]. Premium features may be locked, but the paywall itself always has a visible way out, from its first frame, back to whatever is free [inferred application of STD-visual-details-33 and STD-accessibility-motion-24]; so OpenDesigner does not recommend a hard paywall or a delayed close, even where one app reports that they won [S-L19-111]. Exit-intent and win-back screens count toward the cancel flow's length, which must stay no longer than sign-up (DC-L13-15's hard-to-cancel lint and the DSA example) [inferred]; ClassPass is the example to avoid [S-L19-104]. Steep discounts only for win-back, never straight after onboarding [S-L19-106]. A "one-time" offer must really be one-time; one that returns after it was said to be gone is fake scarcity [inferred mapping]. Candidate checks: (1) an engagement feature (reminder, usage nudge, streak prompt) with no off switch: warning [inferred]; (2) an upsell attached to a usage or guilt message: human review as confirmshaming [inferred mapping]; (3) a paywall or account wall in front of content promoted as free: human review; (4) a lapse that removes progress or blocks content: human review; (5) new: a cancel flow with more screens than sign-up, counting exit-intent and win-back screens: warning (DC-L13-15's own lint, now with a real example [S-L19-104]); (6) new: a paywall or offer whose close control is missing or delayed: error (STD-accessibility-motion-24) [S-L19-111]; (7) new: a prize wheel or lottery with a fixed outcome: human review as fake urgency or scarcity [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106] [inferred mapping]; (8) new: prices that vary by device or network: human review, since no source weighs their fairness [S-L19-106]. Evidence strength: the satire [S-L19-048] mocks pressure and the paywall consultant pushes back on it (he has a hard time accepting the prize wheel and says it may not suit a long-term business) [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106], for different reasons, so two channels agree; [S-L19-104] and [S-L19-106] are one interview; the Moonly results are one app's; DC-L13-15 supplies the policy and legal anchors.
evidence: [S-L19-048] [S-L19-079] [S-L19-061] [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106] [S-L19-108] [S-L19-111]. Compared against DC-L13-15, DC-L19-37, DC-L19-83, DC-L19-98, DC-L19-106, DC-L19-114 and DC-L19-155 (store rules and where people pay).

Suggested addition to the `enforced` label: "every paywall and offer shows its close control from the start" [inferred].
- Q-pattern-05 visual samples: the anti-pattern gallery (the 342-videos message with an upsell, the step-goal pop-up with a button suggesting a lower goal, the streak punishment) [S-L19-048] beside an upgrade prompt that slides the higher limit in [S-L19-079]; a spin-the-wheel paywall beside a trial timeline [S-L19-104]; ClassPass as a count, under five screens to join against 17 to cancel [S-L19-104]; per-feature paywalls beside one paywall that unlocks everything [S-L19-111].
impact now / as it grows:
- *Prompt at the limit:* now slightly less conversion pressure. It keeps trust as the user base grows [inferred].
- *Many moments, one offer:* now one paywall to maintain. New gated features reuse it instead of adding paywalls, so the message "one plan unlocks everything" holds as features grow [S-L19-111] [inferred].

- *Off switch:* now one setting per feature. As engagement features multiply, a settings page of switches keeps people in control (STD-visual-details-39).

title: Progress, streaks and rewards
questions: (questions the designer answers) Does the product show progress toward the person's own goals? Does it add a streak, a currency, badges or leaderboards? If a streak, which feeling brings people back: fear of losing it, optimism, attachment to a character, or a visible chain of days? What must someone do each day to keep it, and what happens when they miss a day? What does the product prove before it asks for effort?
options:
- **None:** the product's value is the reason to return. For everyday work tools the house standard is to remove friction rather than add delight (STD-when-to-animate-20).
- **Progress only:** show what has been done and what is left, as Exercism shows the share of a language completed [S-L19-078]; a percentage, not "in progress" [S-L19-086]; multi-step flows show position and total (the L13 goal-gradient default).
- **A streak, and the feeling it leans on (new):** Mobbin's review of 859 streak designs sorts them by lever [S-L19-105]. *Fear of loss:* more urgent copy, a countdown clock and a mascot that makes you feel guilty. *Optimism:* encouraging copy, a button reworded as a promise to yourself, and milestones collected as proof of progress (Opal). *Attachment:* a mascot that cheers you on or grows alongside you. *Visual attention:* days shown as a visible chain in which a gap stands out at once. The video describes the fear lever without endorsing it and asks whether streaks build habits or only make people afraid to stop [S-L19-105]. The copy is DC-L19-37's decision, the commitment button's label DC-L19-38's and DC-L19-104's, and the mascot DC-L19-77's.
- **Flexible streak rules (new):** Duolingo's streak freeze lets people miss a day without losing everything; allowing up to two equipped at a time raised daily active learners by 0.38%, over 200,000 more people a day. A variant where one lesson keeps the streak alive beat one that required the full daily goal, with over 40% more people keeping a 7-day streak. Apps increasingly offer repairs, freezes, pauses and grace days, designing for recovery rather than perfection [S-L19-105]. The video cites an unnamed study in which missing a day had almost no effect on whether a habit became automatic [S-L19-105].
- **The habit loop as a checklist (new):** cue (a reminder that shows the streak number, before the app is opened), craving (a short sound after each session, like Duolingo's jingle), response (make the next step easy, such as auto-advancing) and reward. Once the streak is routine the reward loses its pull, so apps add surprises such as animations, milestone celebrations and bonus XP [S-L19-105]; how much of that the house allows is DC-L19-83's decision.
- **A game layer:** one central currency earned by the core actions (Duolingo XP, Todoist Karma) that shows progress; a streak kept alive by the core action; rewards scaled to the size of the goal; badges for milestones such as 30 days in a row; short quizzes that pay the currency. Rewards must tie to real goals, because meaningless rewards motivate no one [S-L19-078].
- **A metric of its own (new):** a named measure people adopt in their own words: streaks (Duolingo), a readiness score (Oura), closing the rings (Apple). The video claims, without data, that people who talk in the metric rarely switch products [S-L19-110]. Recaps and highlights package the stats: Origin's weekly recap and daily brief, and Runner's post-run highlights, which give a sense of accomplishment [S-L19-110].
- **A social layer:** leaderboards and public badges; a league with promotion, neutral and demotion zones (Duolingo); a local leaderboard when the ranking involves money, to account for income and currency differences [S-L19-078].
- **Sharing as a reason to come back** [inferred framing]: in a yearly recap, the share button is always visible because sharing is why the recap succeeds; one share button with scopes (slide, chapter, whole recap); the owner's name on shared content; a short comparison with last year [S-L19-076]. New: Opal turns screen-time insights into a swipeable story people share [S-L19-110]; Moonly offers a ready-made one-tap share flow when someone takes a screenshot, because people share insights about themselves, not features, and reports that 23% of users share something [S-L19-111].
- **Rejected:** punishing a broken streak [S-L19-048]; meaningless rewards [S-L19-078]; fear and guilt as the lever [S-L19-105], which DC-L19-37 rules out as tone aimed at the person; making streaks stricter after people lapse, the obvious fix that Duolingo found worked worse than flexibility [S-L19-105]. Removing choices so the core action needs no decision works for TikTok because its algorithm learns what people want [S-L19-077]; the research warns that choice overload averages near zero and does not justify deleting options (L13 choice-overload row), and lists addictive design among the patterns to watch (DC-L13-15).
visual effect: Visible progress and a single currency give a sense of momentum [S-L19-078]; leaderboards add comparison and pressure [S-L19-078] [inferred for "pressure"]; punishments make the product feel hostile [S-L19-048]. A chain of days makes a gap visible at once; urgent copy, a countdown and a guilty mascot create fear and guilt; encouraging copy and collectible milestones make progress feel like building a better self [S-L19-105].
depends on: audience and use (Q-aud-01, Q-scope-06), how lively the brand is (Q-brand-04), the deceptive-pattern policy (DC-L13-15), tone (DC-L19-37), the mascot (DC-L19-77, Q-img-04), the commitment button label (DC-L19-104), sound (Q-motion-08), onboarding order (DC-L19-129: value before the game).
affects: progress bar or ring, streak counter, a day chain or calendar, streak freeze, repair and grace-day controls, badge, leaderboard, currency counter, recap and highlights, share sheet, milestone celebrations (DC-L19-130), reminder notifications and their settings, glance views (Q-pattern-06) [inferred].
token encoding: none new. Counters use tabular digits (STD-visual-details-02) and animate with NumberFlow (STD-visual-details-59); celebrations use the expressive motion set (DC-L04-19).
platform notes: a milestone may get one success haptic, never one per frame or on scroll (STD-springs-gestures-61). A reminder that shows the streak number is the cue before the app is opened [S-L19-105]; a streak or goal is a candidate for a widget or complication (Q-pattern-06) [inferred]. A completion sound fits Q-motion-08's `rare-events` option, behind mute, and never as the only signal (STD-springs-gestures-61, STD-accessibility-motion-20) [inferred].
accessibility constraints: progress rings and bars show the value in text; a day chain also says it in words ("5 of 7 days") rather than by filled color alone [inferred]; league zones are not marked by color alone; celebrations respect reduced motion (STD-accessibility-motion-02); nothing is lost to a time limit the person cannot extend (WCAG 2.2.1) [inferred], which freezes and grace days help with [inferred link].
default: (default + heuristic) `none` for work tools; `progress` for products built around the person's own goals; a streak or a game or social layer only with an explicit goal, and then with these conditions: optimism or a visible chain as the lever, never fear or guilt [S-L19-105] (DC-L19-37); one unit of the core action keeps the streak alive; freezes, repairs or grace days built in [S-L19-105]; the milestone is celebrated and the daily completion only confirmed (DC-L19-83); rewards tie to real goals and value is shown before any game [S-L19-078]; reminders and other engagement features have an off switch [inferred, generalising the three off switches in S-L19-048]; progress is honest, with no artificial head start (the L13 goal-gradient ethics note). The rule that a missed day is never punished rested on satire [S-L19-048]; Duolingo's reported results now back it [S-L19-105], so two channels agree. Judge a streak by whether people come back after a break and reach their goal, not by daily engagement alone, because the video warns that engagement is not the same as a lasting habit [S-L19-105] (DC-L19-137). Differs from [S-L19-105] on one point: it explains the visible chain with the Zeigarnik effect, which the L13 research marks as a failed replication. The chain can stay, because people do tend to resume unfinished tasks (the Ovsiankina tendency in the L13 table), but no reminder or nag may be justified by Zeigarnik (the L13 "no nag" rule). The Duolingo figures come from the video without a linked study; the claim that a coined metric stops people switching has no data [S-L19-110].
evidence: [S-L19-078] [S-L19-086] [S-L19-076] [S-L19-048] [S-L19-077] [S-L19-105] [S-L19-110] [S-L19-111]. Compared against DC-L13-15, the L13 goal-gradient, peak-end, choice-overload and Zeigarnik rows, DC-L19-37, DC-L19-77, DC-L19-83 and DC-L19-104.
maps to:
- New question (proposed Q-pattern-12, zoom 3, stage 23, show if Q-aud-01 is `regular` or `large`): "Should the product use progress, streaks or rewards to bring people back?" Options `none` (default when Q-scope-06 is `operate`), `progress` (default otherwise), new `streak` ("a streak kept by one unit of the core action, with freezes or grace days") [S-L19-105], `game-layer`, `social` [inferred defaults].
- Q-pattern-12 heuristic (new): "A streak never punishes a missed day and never leans on fear or guilt; celebrate the milestone, confirm the day" [S-L19-105] [S-L19-048]; the last clause is DC-L19-83's rule, not the video's [inferred].
- Q-pattern-05: fear-based streak screens (countdowns, guilt) are a human-review item; a lint cannot catch them, because a streak's end-of-day deadline is real [inferred].
- Visual samples: a fear-based streak screen beside an optimism-based one [S-L19-105]; a streak freeze and a day chain with one gap [S-L19-105]; the savings app's goal home, league leaderboard with promotion and demotion zones, and analytics with overspending marked [S-L19-078]; the recap with one share button and three scopes [S-L19-076]; Opal's story-format insights [S-L19-110].
impact now / as it grows:
- *None:* now nothing to maintain. Return visits depend entirely on the product's value.
- *Progress:* now one bar per goal. It stays honest and cheap as goals multiply [inferred].
- *Flexible streak:* now a daily cue and a few rules (freeze, repair, grace day). The longer a streak runs, the more it becomes part of people's identity, which is why losing one makes some people quit [S-L19-105]; recovery rules keep them coming back.
- *Game layer:* now motivating. Every new feature must be priced in the currency, and the economy needs balancing as it grows [inferred].
- *Metric of its own:* now a name to define and explain. It becomes vocabulary the product must keep stable as features change [inferred].
- *Social layer:* now adds comparison. As users grow, fairness (local boards, leagues) and moderation become work [S-L19-078] [inferred for moderation].
- *Sharing:* now one share control. Each shared item carries the brand to new people [S-L19-076] [S-L19-111] [inferred for the brand].
standards: STD-when-to-animate-04, STD-when-to-animate-09, STD-when-to-animate-20, STD-springs-gestures-61, STD-accessibility-motion-02, STD-accessibility-motion-20, STD-visual-details-02, STD-visual-details-59, STD-visual-details-39, STD-visual-details-44, STD-visual-details-45, STD-visual-details-47

title: Measuring whether a design change worked
questions: (questions the designer answers) What is this page or flow for: sales, sign-ups, enquiries, subscriptions? Which number should the change move, and which number must not get worse? How will we check it: analytics before and after, an A/B test, or a usability test? What gets tested first? Who can see the analytics?
options:
- **Not measured:** the page is judged on looks. The source says clients mostly judge looks while users care whether it works, and a site that looks good but serves no purpose still won't sell [S-L19-038]. An ugly, text-heavy paywall beat every polished design for one app [S-L19-104], so looks alone do not predict results.
- **Before and after:** compare the site's analytics before and after the new design ships; build the site yourself or keep view-only access so you can [S-L19-038]. Weaker than a controlled test, because other things change over time [inferred].
- **Controlled A/B test:** when you build option A and option B, validate them and ship the winner, not both (STD-when-to-animate-22); break a familiar pattern only with proof, and test rather than assume (STD-visual-details-37). A/B tests and analytics need large traffic (L13 methods table). New, from practice: keep the current screen as the control and test four to five new designs against it; some wins needed a second or third experiment to become statistically significant [S-L19-106]. Moonly runs hundreds of tests a month, uses AI tools to reconcile its analytics and recommend ship, don't ship or collect more data, and reports its paywall going from 10% conversion in 2020 to 40% on paid traffic through small, almost daily tests in which every element had to win its place [S-L19-111].
- **Usability testing only:** about five people per round finds most problems (L13 methods table), but the samples of small pre-launch tests are too small to prove impact [S-L19-038].
- **A main number plus a guard number (new):** pick the main number by the kind of business: ARPU for an app built to launch fast and gather users, LTV and retention for a long-term business, because weekly plans can show a $3-4 ARPU while monthly churn runs at 90-95% [S-L19-106]. For a paywall the consultant also watches the share of installs that reach the paywall (above 80% is good, 90% or more excellent), trial-to-paid conversion, day-1, day-7 and day-30 retention, and churn [S-L19-106]. Retention and LTV matter more than the first payment [S-L19-104], and engagement is not the same as a lasting habit [S-L19-105].
- **What to test first (new):** radically different designs first (a video, a bullet list, a trial timeline, a long-form page), then personalisation, then how plans and prices are packaged, with device-based pricing last because it is the most work for the smallest gain [S-L19-106] [S-L19-104]. Moonly's founder calls pricing tests the most important and images the biggest lever [S-L19-111]. The two run different products, and both say to test rather than assume.
- **Validate the market first (new):** a lean web funnel before building the full app, for fast signals at low cost [S-L19-111].
- **Where to spend effort:** for a site with heavy traffic, conversion rate optimisation beats more SEO, because a small gain at that scale is worth a lot [S-L19-038].
- **Reporting:** short case studies with the services, the problem, and the solution with numbers [S-L19-038].
visual effect: none on screen (a process decision). Recorded metrics sit next to the decisions they belong to, so later sessions know what each change was for [inferred].
depends on: what the screens are for (Q-scope-06), the system-level success measures (Q-gov-05, DC-L11-20), which measure adoption of the design system rather than product outcomes, DC-L19-166, which proposes product results before and after as one way to judge the whole system, and the paywall and onboarding decisions whose results are measured (DC-L19-139, DC-L19-129, DC-L19-136).
affects: `opendesigner/decisions.md` entries, DESIGN.md, the deceptive-pattern policy (conversion pressure is where DC-L13-15 gets tested), A/B variant prototypes.
token encoding: none (process). A decision can carry `expected_effect { metric, guard_metric, baseline, check: "before-after" | "ab-test" | "usability" }`, mirroring DC-L11-20's `metrics[]` shape [inferred].
platform notes: most website builders include basic analytics [S-L19-038]; the paywall metrics above come from consumer phone apps [S-L19-106] [S-L19-111]. App-store analytics tools are not covered by any source.
accessibility constraints: no variant may drop below the floors to win a test: both A and B pass WCAG 2.2 AA contrast, 24 px targets, visible focus and reduced motion [inferred]; a trick that raises conversion is still a deceptive pattern (DC-L13-15): the paywall consultant says a spin-the-wheel offer works for short-term weekly revenue but may not suit a long-term business [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106], and the paywall video's narrator adds that people stop believing fake urgency once every app uses it [S-L19-104].
default: (default + heuristic) For `persuade` screens and paywalls, record the one number each major change is meant to move, plus one guard number that must not get worse (retention or churn next to a conversion number) [S-L19-106] [S-L19-105] [inferred proposal]; check it before and after at minimum; run a controlled test only with enough traffic, test big differences before details, and ship the winner (STD-when-to-animate-22); never claim impact from a five-person test. The first version of this card rested on one freelancer's video [S-L19-038]; the practice of testing against a control now also comes from a paywall consultant [S-L19-106] and an app founder [S-L19-111] on another channel, backed by two house standards and the L13 methods table. The consultant's percentages and "four to five variants" are one practitioner's habits, not thresholds. No research card covers product experiments (DC-L11-20 measures the system). DC-L19-166 uses the same kind of evidence for a system-level check; this card works per change.
evidence: [S-L19-038] [S-L19-104] [S-L19-105] [S-L19-106] [S-L19-111]. Compared against DC-L11-20, DC-L13-15, DC-L19-166 and the L13 Part D methods table.
maps to:
- New question (proposed Q-pattern-13, zoom 3, show if Q-scope-06 is `persuade` or the product sells plans): "Which number should this page move, and how will you check it?" Options `not-measured`, `before-after` (default), `ab-test`, `usability-only`. The answer is saved with the decision, together with two new fields: the guard number, and the kind of business (quick launch or long-term), which decides the main number [S-L19-106].
- Q-pattern-13 heuristic (new): "Test big differences before details; judge a win by the main number and the guard number together" [S-L19-106] [S-L19-105].
- Q-gov-05: new note, "DC-L19-166's `outcomes` option judges the system by product results before and after; the per-change numbers recorded by Q-pattern-13 feed it".
- Visual samples: a short case-study card with services, problem, and solution with numbers [S-L19-038]; a paywall experiment laid out as the control plus four to five variants [S-L19-106] [inferred layout].
impact now / as it grows:
- *Not measured:* now no setup. Design arguments stay matters of taste as the team grows [inferred].
- *Before and after:* now needs analytics access. It gives a rough signal that gets noisier as more changes ship at once [inferred].
- *A/B test:* now needs traffic and tooling. It scales best, because each change is judged on its own (STD-when-to-animate-22); at Moonly's pace it also needs help reconciling the numbers [S-L19-111].
- *Usability only:* now cheap and fast for finding problems. It never proves impact, however many rounds are run [S-L19-038].
- *Main number plus guard:* now one more number to watch. As tests pile up, it stops wins that lift conversion while churn rises [S-L19-106] [inferred].
standards: STD-when-to-animate-22, STD-visual-details-37, STD-visual-details-44

title: AI workspace components beyond labels
questions: (questions the designer answers) If the product generates content, does it keep a searchable history? If the AI remembers things, can people see and edit that memory? Can people edit part of a response in place? What shows while the AI works? Are confidence levels shown? Can people ask the AI why a number on a dashboard changed? Does an AI product need onboarding at all?
options:
(all from one Kole Jain video [S-L19-055] unless noted)
- **A prompt box as the front door:** a large prompt box above the fold gets people trying the tool at once; ChatGPT and Gemini dropped their landing pages. A useful box previews attached PDFs and images, compresses long pasted code into a block, offers context chips that change the mode, integration buttons, and progressive disclosure such as an advanced toggle or a cost estimate above the input.
- **Generation history:** called essential when the product outputs text, code or images; organised by session or tied to the source block, with a first-line preview, deletion, and search, which turns history into a workspace.
- **Memory panel:** if the AI has persistent memory, it must be visible and under the user's control: see storage, bulk delete, add facts. The source criticises tools that hide it in settings.
- **Inline editing:** highlight any part of a response and type the change (Claude, Lex, Notion AI).
- **While it works:** short, looping, fluid loaders; streamed output; skeletons with shimmer; a trail of steps (documents retrieved, sources cited) fading in one by one (see DC-L19-127).
- **Confidence indicator:** a pill under each response ("high confidence", "unverified"), clickable for the number.
- **A dark "soft glass" look:** a style trend, not a pattern; it falls under the house rules for translucency.
- **AI that explains the data (new):** people staring at a dashboard ask why a number changed; AI fills that gap as a single prompt right below a chart or a full AI layer beside the data. AI dashboards get about twice the saves and exports of the average dashboard screen on Mobbin, which shows what designers collect, not what users prefer [S-L19-110].
- **Little or no onboarding (new):** for AI chat the first prompt is where people find value, so letting them in fast may be best; only 7% of AI apps personalise during onboarding, letting the product learn from use instead [S-L19-107] (DC-L19-129).
- **Offers from the assistant (new):** Moonly's AI guide recommends a paid add-on only when that add-on can really help the person at that moment [S-L19-111] (DC-L19-135). How the assistant looks is DC-L19-78's decision.
visual effect: History and memory make the tool feel like a workspace; inline edits feel like revising, not regenerating; a step trail makes the AI feel like a collaborator rather than a black box; streaming turns delay into anticipation [S-L19-055].
depends on: Q-ai-01 (whether and how AI appears), DC-L13-16 (AI interface patterns), DC-L08-22 (AI module), wait feedback (DC-L19-127), dashboard charts (DC-L19-122), onboarding (DC-L19-129).
affects: prompt input, attachment chip, context chips, history list with search, memory panel, inline-edit popover, streaming text container, skeleton, step trail, confidence badge, an "ask about this chart" prompt.
token encoding: existing AI roles (`color.ai.*`, `icon.ai`) and thinking-indicator motion from DC-L13-16; nothing new [inferred].
platform notes: the examples are web and desktop AI tools; no source covers native mobile AI patterns.
accessibility constraints: streamed text must not flood screen readers, and the view must not autoscroll to the end (DC-L13-16); the step trail and confidence level are text, not color alone; glass surfaces become frostier or solid under reduced transparency (STD-accessibility-motion-11), and text on them gets higher contrast (STD-visual-details-13); memory and history deletion are undoable or confirmed, as with any destructive action (STD-visual-details-40).
default: (default + heuristic) For products whose Q-ai-01 answer is `chat` or `presence-mode`: a prompt box with attachment previews, searchable history, streamed output, and the stop, regenerate, edit and copy controls DC-L13-16 already asks for. A memory panel is required whenever the AI keeps memory [S-L19-055]; this fits the house rule to add previews, confirmations and disclaimers to AI features (STD-visual-details-45) [inferred link]. Two points differ from the source and follow DC-L13-16: a step trail may show retrieval steps and citations, but not narrated reasoning presented as an explanation; and confidence labels belong in high-stakes contexts, not under every response. For data products, a prompt under charts that answers "why did this change?" is worth offering [S-L19-110], and its answer names the data and period it used, with no narrated reasoning presented as explanation (DC-L13-16) [inferred application]. An AI chat product can skip onboarding when the first prompt is the value (DC-L19-129) [S-L19-107]. The workspace parts are one creator's survey of current tools [S-L19-055]; the dashboard AI trend is one Mobbin presenter's observation [S-L19-110].
maps to:
- Q-ai-01: new follow-up (zoom 3, show if Q-ai-01 is not `none`), multi-select "Which AI workspace parts does the product need?": `history`, `memory-panel`, `inline-edit`, `step-trail`, `confidence`, and new `explain-data` ("a prompt under charts that answers why a number changed") [S-L19-110]; default `history` for `chat`, and `explain-data` when Q-layout-03 is `data` [inferred].
- Q-ai-01: new heuristic, "memory that exists is shown and editable". New heuristic: "an AI answer about data names the data and period it used" [inferred from S-L19-110 and DC-L13-16].
- Visual samples: a prompt box with attachment previews and context chips; a research trail fading in step by step; a confidence pill under an answer [S-L19-055].
impact now / as it grows:
- *Prompt box and history:* now the core of the product. Search keeps history useful as generations pile up [S-L19-055].
- *Memory panel:* now one more screen. As memory grows, people need bulk delete and storage limits to stay in control [S-L19-055].
- *Inline edit:* now faster fixes. Each new output type (code, images) needs its own way to select a part [inferred].
- *Step trail and confidence:* now more trust. They have to stay honest as models change, or they mislead (DC-L13-16).
- *Explain the data:* now a prompt under charts. As data sources multiply, each answer must say what it used, or it misleads [inferred].
