title: Asking for system permissions, notifications first
questions: (questions the designer answers) When the app needs a system permission, such as notifications, does it show the system dialog straight away or explain first? At which moment does it ask? What happens after someone says "not now"?
options:
- **The system dialog alone, at the moment of need:** the operating system's pop-up with nothing of the product's own before it. The onboarding study mentions it only as the thing a primer goes in front of, and does not recommend it [S-L19-107].
- **An explaining screen first (a primer):** many apps show a custom screen before the notification pop-up, which the video says improves accept rates significantly, hedged with "apparently" and no figure. Brilliant's primer says it will remind you to learn so learning becomes a habit [S-L19-107].
- **A primer that previews the notification:** an app captioned as Center also shows the notification you would receive if you allow it [S-L19-107].
- **Rejected: every permission on first launch** [inferred]: the house rule asks for private data at the right moment, only for what is needed, and openly [S-L19-020] (STD-visual-details-41), which a batch of prompts before any use cannot do.
- **Timing (for any option):** ask when the benefit is concrete. Blinkist's trial timeline promises a reminder before the trial ends, and push opt-ins rose along with trial sign-ups [S-L19-104]; Kole Jain's savings app pairs its onboarding request to connect a bank with reassurance that the app won't steal people's money [S-L19-078], the same move for a data request inside the product [inferred link].
visual effect: System dialog alone: a bare system box out of context. Primer: a screen or card in the product's own look with one benefit sentence, an image or a sample notification, and two buttons [inferred layout from the Brilliant and Center examples]. With a preview: people see exactly what they agree to. Mobile flows carry more of these screens than web ones; the video suggests this "might explain" why web onboarding runs 21% shorter than iOS [S-L19-107].
depends on: Q-plat-01 (`ios`, `android`; a desktop app with ambient features, DC-L19-149, has prompts too [inferred]), DC-L19-129 (onboarding order), the product's reason to notify (reminders, trial ends, messages).
affects: a permission-primer screen or sheet, onboarding steps, a settings switch to turn the permission on later, reminder copy, the trial-timeline paywall (DC-L19-135).
token encoding: none (a pattern and content decision).
platform notes: the examples are phone apps [S-L19-107] [S-L19-104]; the system dialog itself cannot be styled, so the primer is the only part the design system draws [inferred]. The L08 settings pattern (P9) sends system-level permissions to the system Settings app (HIG), so a later "turn on" link goes there [inferred application]. No source covers web push permission.
accessibility constraints: the primer is an ordinary screen or dialog with a way out (STD-accessibility-motion-24, STD-visual-details-33); "Not now" is a real button, not a faint link, because DC-L13-15 lints unequal accept and decline in consent dialogs [inferred application]; the benefit is written in text, not only shown in a picture [inferred].
default: (default + heuristic) Default `primer`, shown when the permission starts to pay off for the person (after they set a goal, start a trial or ask for a reminder), with a preview when the notification's content is the selling point. "Not now" is respected: the product asks again only when the person turns on a feature that needs the permission, never on a timer, which would be the nagging DC-L13-15 lints [inferred]. Rule of thumb: ask when people can see what they get, and say it in one line (STD-visual-details-41).
evidence: [S-L19-020] [S-L19-078] [S-L19-104] [S-L19-107]; compared with DC-L13-15, DC-L19-129, DC-L19-135 and the L08 catalog's P9 Settings pattern. The patterns cards, updated in parallel, now send notification primers to DC-L19-129 (DC-L19-135's platform note), whose setup checklist lists "a primer before system permission prompts" and whose default makes "Not now" stick. This card agrees with both and adds what they leave open: the timing rule, the preview variant, and permissions asked later in the product, outside onboarding.
maps to:
- New question (proposed Q-plat-16, zoom 3, stage 04, show if Q-plat-01 includes `ios` or `android`): "When the app needs a system permission, such as notifications, how should it ask?" Options `at-need` (the system dialog alone), `primer` (default), `primer-preview`. No up-front option, because it breaks STD-visual-details-41. DC-L19-129's checklist item under its proposed Q-pattern-15 takes its form from this answer, so the choice is made once [inferred].
- Q-pattern-05 (planned): DC-L13-15's "re-prompting after a dismissal" check also covers permission primers [inferred].
- Visual samples: Brilliant's primer and the primer with a notification preview [S-L19-107]; Blinkist's trial timeline, whose reminder day is the reason to allow notifications [S-L19-104].
impact now / as it grows:
- *System dialog alone:* now nothing to design. As it grows, every new permission appears without context, and a refusal is hard to win back [inferred].
- *Primer:* now one reusable screen and one sentence per permission. As it grows, new permissions reuse the component, and the moment each one appears becomes a written rule.
- *Primer with preview:* now a sample notification per type. As it grows, the previews must follow the real notification copy.
- *Everything up front (rejected):* now one onboarding stop. As it grows, the list of asks gets longer and each refusal is made before people know why [inferred].
standards: STD-visual-details-41, STD-visual-details-39, STD-visual-details-33, STD-accessibility-motion-24

title: Store rules and where people pay
block path: Platforms > Mobile > App store rules and payment surface
questions: (questions the designer answers) Do people pay through the App Store or Google Play, on the web, or both? Which paywall patterns will the store reject? Should the product start as a web funnel before there is an app?
options:
- **Store purchase only:** the platform's own purchase flow. Moonly found that with native payments half of all cancellations came within 3 minutes of buying, because iOS made cancelling a one-tap habit [S-L19-111]. Moonly is one bootstrapped app, and its founder's figures are self-reported.
- **Store purchase plus web checkout, where the market allows it:** Moonly added Stripe as an alternative for US iPhone users, with a small discount; the founder says LTV doubled overnight, and the host says about 80% of US customers now pay that way [S-L19-111]. The video is inconsistent: the host says US payments moved off Apple entirely, the guest calls Stripe an alternative.
- **Android alternative billing through Google's SDK:** the same founder advises against it: the app controls nothing, the screen is built to put people off, and without Google Pay people must type their card details, which he says kills almost all conversions [S-L19-111].
- **Web funnel first, app later:** validate the market with a lean web funnel, which gives more freedom and instant signals, before spending on the full app [S-L19-111]. In Mobbin's sample, web onboarding is also shorter than iOS, partly because of the permission and paywall screens mobile carries (hedged in the source) [S-L19-107].
- **What the store allows on the paywall (applies to every option):** in early 2026 Apple started rejecting paywall patterns that relied on free-trial toggles, some of which it considered confusing or misleading [S-L19-104]; this is one video's report of dated App Review behaviour, with no second source. The paywall designer prefers a longer trial to aggressive last-minute discounts partly to stay compliant and safe, and is waiting to see how Apple treats seasonal sales [S-L19-104]; Slopes' "pay ramp", one "redeem your free week" action, borrows Apple's redeem-free-trial approach [S-L19-104]. This gives DC-L13-15's platform note ("app-store review rules also police some patterns [inferred; not verified here]") its first source.
visual effect: Store purchase: a system sheet people already know, quick to buy and quick to cancel [S-L19-111]. Web checkout: the product's own form in its own look, with more fields; a wallet button spares the typing, and its absence is what the founder blames for failed Android conversions [S-L19-111]. Web funnel: a phone-sized web flow of questions and a checkout, built with DC-L19-144's app-shell posture [inferred].
depends on: Q-plat-01, Q-plat-02 (`phone`), the owner's business model and markets (owner inputs, never assumed), DC-L19-134 (pricing), DC-L19-135 (paywall ethics and its Q-pattern-05 checks), DC-L19-139 (the paywall screen), DC-L13-15.
affects: the paywall's plan picker (avoid a trial toggle on iOS), a checkout form (card fields, wallet buttons), the subscription-management and cancel flow, fine-print copy, the screens of a mobile web funnel.
token encoding: none (a business and policy decision). The store rules become builder checks, kept with DC-L13-15's lint rules in `$extensions` or config.
platform notes: payment and review rules differ by store, country and year. The sources describe US iOS and Google's alternative billing as of 2026 [S-L19-111] and Apple's early-2026 rejections [S-L19-104]; the builder presents them as dated facts to re-check [inferred]. Two more store-shaped levers appear: custom App Store product pages that match the ad a person came from and lead into a matching onboarding flow [S-L19-111], and prices set by device, network and battery state, which the paywall consultant calls one of the last levers because it is so much work [S-L19-106]. Neither source asks whether device-based prices are fair [inferred], so the builder does not offer them.
accessibility constraints: a web checkout follows the form rules: inputs at 16px or more so iOS Safari does not zoom (STD-mobile-touch-11), the right keyboard per field (STD-mobile-touch-13), visible labels and error text (DC-L19-110, DC-L19-111); a paywall always has a way out (STD-visual-details-33, STD-accessibility-motion-24).
default: (default + heuristic) Default `store-only`, recorded as an owner input; web checkout only when the owner confirms their store and market allow it. Rules whatever the choice: avoid a free-trial toggle on an iOS paywall, because Apple began rejecting some in early 2026 [S-L19-104] (one video's dated report, to re-check before relying on it, as DC-L19-106 and DC-L19-139 also say); a web checkout keeps cancelling as easy as subscribing, since DC-L13-15 flags a cancel flow with more steps than sign-up and cites the EU DSA's example of termination made harder than subscribing [inferred application; the source does not say whether harder cancelling explains any of Stripe's higher LTV]; a discount for paying on the web is shown as a discount [inferred]. Rule of thumb: the store decides what the paywall may show, the owner decides where money changes hands, and the system keeps both honest.
evidence: [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106] [S-L19-107] [S-L19-111]; compared with DC-L13-15, DC-L19-106, DC-L19-134, DC-L19-135, DC-L19-139, DC-L19-144. The patterns and components cards, updated in parallel, now carry the paywall side of the same Mobbin facts (DC-L19-139 lists trial toggles as rejected on iOS, DC-L19-106 carries the switch rule, DC-L19-135 owns the Q-pattern-05 checks); this card owns only where money changes hands and the store rules around it.
maps to:
- New question (proposed Q-plat-17, zoom 3, stage 04, show if Q-plat-01 includes `ios` or `android` and the owner says the app charges money): "How will people pay: through the App Store or Google Play, on the web, or both?" Options `store-only` (default), `store-plus-web`, `web-first`; recorded with `--set-by chosen` and never `assumed`, because it is an owner input.
- Q-pattern-05 (planned): the checks are DC-L19-135's. This card asks that its check 5 (a cancel flow longer than sign-up, a warning) also count a web checkout's cancel path [inferred], and proposes one more: "a free-trial toggle on an iOS paywall" as a warning that asks to re-check Apple's current rules, not an error, because its only source is one video's dated report [S-L19-104].
- Q-plat-01: new heuristic for consumer subscription products: a lean web funnel can test the market before the app is built [S-L19-111] (one founder's advice; confirms the default `web`).
- Visual sample: the same paywall footer with a free-trial toggle, marked "Apple began rejecting some of these in early 2026 (re-check)", beside a trial timeline and Slopes' single "redeem your free week" action [S-L19-104].
impact now / as it grows:
- *Store only:* now the least to build, with purchase and refunds handled by the store [inferred]. As it grows, the product keeps the store's one-tap cancel, which Moonly blamed for its early cancellations [S-L19-111].
- *Store plus web:* now a second checkout, its form and its cancel path. As it grows, two billing systems must stay in step (prices, receipts, what each person has unlocked), and each market's rules must be checked again [inferred].
- *Android alternative billing:* now a flow the product cannot design. As it grows, the founder expects it to keep losing conversions [S-L19-111].
- *Web funnel first:* now fast, cheap market signals. As it grows, the app must keep the funnel's promises and carry its accounts and purchases over [inferred].
standards: STD-mobile-touch-11, STD-mobile-touch-13, STD-visual-details-33, STD-accessibility-motion-24

title: Accounts on phones: none, the platform's sign-in, or an email account
questions: (questions the designer answers) Does the product need an account at all? If it does, which sign-in comes first? At which point in the flow is it asked for?
options:
- **No account; the device keeps the data:** Moonly has 10 million users and no login screen. Its data sits in the Apple keychain and follows people to a new iPhone, and collecting emails was not paying off. Only 12% of apps on Mobbin have no sign-up or login step anywhere [S-L19-111].
- **The platform's own sign-in:** people are used to signing in with Apple and hiding their real email address [S-L19-111].
- **Email, or a phone number with a code:** typing a real email adds real mental effort, and SMS codes do not always arrive in seconds, which the founder calls a UX nightmare [S-L19-111]. When a form is needed, one app (captioned as House) split its sign-up across several screens and saw 15% more conversions, and a password field can tick off each rule as people type [S-L19-107].
- **When the account is asked for (any of the above):** first, before anything, which is the sign up, set up, aha order the onboarding video describes; after trying the core experience (an app captioned as Elma; Duolingo's first lesson, 60 screens before an account); after a couple of personalization questions (Tide) [S-L19-107]; or just before the paywall, so the subscription is tied to a user ID, which the paywall consultant prefers although his tests of the order were inconclusive [S-L19-106]. How the sign-up screens are written (an escape to log in, verification that blocks or reminds) and when the account is asked for stay with DC-L19-129; this card adds whether an account is needed at all and which sign-in comes first.
visual effect: No account: the app opens straight into use. Platform sign-in: one button and one system sheet. Email or phone: a form, a wait for a code and a verification step, so more screens stand between people and the product.
depends on: Q-plat-01 (the keychain route is the source's iPhone example), Q-plat-07 (data that must follow people to other platforms), DC-L19-129, DC-L19-155 (purchases tied to an account), owner inputs (what data must sync, whether email marketing is planned).
affects: onboarding order, sign-in and sign-up screens, password and code fields, account settings, restoring data and purchases on a new device [inferred].
token encoding: none (a product and pattern decision).
platform notes: the keychain carry-over is Apple's [S-L19-111]; a web product has no device store that follows people, so data that must reach the web or another platform needs an account [inferred].
accessibility constraints: WCAG 2.2 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (AA, in DC-L13-14's list): no memory or transcription test without an alternative such as paste, a password manager or the platform's sign-in [inferred mapping]; password rules change as text, not by color alone [inferred]; on the web, inputs at 16px or more and the right keyboard (`type="email"`, a numeric keyboard for codes) (STD-mobile-touch-11, STD-mobile-touch-13).
default: (default + heuristic) Default: start with the founder's question, why does this product need an account at all [S-L19-111]. No account while the device can keep the data and nothing has to sync; when an account is needed, offer the platform's sign-in first and, when the core can run without an account, ask after people have felt the product [S-L19-107] [inferred ranking]; ask for an email only with the reason in view (STD-visual-details-41). Rule of thumb: an account has to earn its screen.
maps to:
- No new timing question: DC-L19-129 (updated in parallel) now proposes Q-pattern-15, "When should people create an account, and what does setup ask first?", with `account-first`, `after-first-use`, `after-personalising` and `no-account`, recorded as `chosen`. This card adds to it: a fifth option, `before-paywall`, for products that tie the subscription to a user ID [S-L19-106]; a heuristic that recommends `no-account` when the device can keep the data and nothing has to sync [S-L19-111] [inferred]; and a follow-up, "Which sign-in comes first?", with `platform` (default), `email` and `phone-code` [S-L19-111] [inferred default].
- Q-plat-01 `ios` option note: "an iPhone app can keep people's data in the keychain without a login" [S-L19-111].
- Visual sample: an app that opens straight into use with no login [S-L19-111] beside Duolingo's order, where the account comes after the first lesson [S-L19-107].
impact now / as it grows:
- *No account:* now no sign-in screens, password resets or support for them. As it grows, a web version, sharing between people or a second platform forces an account and a move of the data already on devices [inferred].
- *Platform sign-in:* now one button and a hidden email address the product must accept. As it grows, people on other platforms need another way in [inferred].
- *Email or phone:* now the most control and a mailing list. As it grows, codes, resets and verification become support work, and Moonly found its email marketing costly [S-L19-111].
- *Asked later in the flow:* now more people reach the product's value before being asked [S-L19-107]. As it grows, whatever people did before signing in must carry over into the account [inferred].
standards: STD-visual-details-41, STD-visual-details-44, STD-mobile-touch-11, STD-mobile-touch-13

title: The Swift token file: where it lives and how it is isolated
block path: Platforms > Implementation > Swift and SwiftUI output
questions: (questions the designer answers) Does the Swift token file go into one app target, or into a package several apps and extensions share? Must tokens be readable from background work and from the SwiftUI code that runs off the main thread? Which Swift version does the project build with?
options:
- **Into the app target, as exported today:** `engine.py export_swift` writes `build/swift/DesignTokens.swift`: a `public enum` namespace (the project prefix, such as `DS`) holding enums of `static let` constants: colors that switch with light and dark, `CGFloat` spacing and radii, Dynamic Type text styles, durations in seconds and `Animation.spring(duration:bounce:)` springs; the export skill says to add it to the iOS target. Differs from the house Swift standards: in an app target that follows STD-swift-17 (Default Actor Isolation set to MainActor, the default for new app projects in Xcode 26 [S-L19-034]), every token becomes main-actor isolated. Reading one in a `@concurrent` function or a nonisolated `Shape.path(in:)` then fails to compile, and inside `.visualEffect` it warns (checked with swiftc 6.4; recorded as conflicts under STD-swift-17, STD-swift-18 and STD-swift-44).
- **Into the app target, marked `nonisolated`:** the namespace, its extension and the color helper marked `nonisolated`, which the recorded check says compiles clean; `nonisolated` on a type covers all its members from Swift 6.1 [S-L19-034]. The tokens stay immutable `static let` constants, the first choice STD-swift-32 gives for globals [inferred].
- **A Swift package shared by several targets:** a library, so its APIs stay nonisolated and callers decide where work runs (STD-swift-18); access control is written out at the boundary (STD-swift-61); and public types meant to be shared are marked `Sendable` explicitly, because public types never get inferred sendability [S-L19-034] (STD-swift-26). A package fits once a second app, a widget or another extension needs the same tokens [inferred].
- **What comes with every option:** code written against the tokens follows the house Swift standard [S-L19-034]: no `@MainActor` on SwiftUI views (STD-swift-43); an animation that answers a gesture starts with `withAnimation` in the synchronous callback, on the event's frame, using the exported springs (STD-swift-45); SwiftUI's `@Sendable` closures copy the one token they need into the capture list (STD-swift-44); shared state such as a theme uses `@Observable` (STD-swift-97) [inferred application]; new tests use Swift Testing (STD-swift-75) and logs use `Logger` (STD-swift-88).
visual effect: where the file lives changes nothing on screen. STD-swift-45 is the part people feel: an animation that answers a finger starts on the same frame as the touch [S-L19-034].
depends on: Q-plat-01 (`ios`, or `desktop` for a Mac app), Q-plat-08 (`swiftui`), Q-plat-09 (OS floor and toolchain), Q-plat-07 (what the platforms share), DC-L10-20, DC-L10-22, DC-L19-148.
affects: `build/swift/DesignTokens.swift`, the export skill's install step, SwiftUI component code, widgets and other extensions [inferred], tests, the AGENTS snippet's pointer to the Swift standard.
token encoding: the Swift export as it stands: `DS.Colors.*` (`Color`), `DS.Space.*` and `DS.Radius.*` (`CGFloat`), `DS.Typography.*` (`Font` text styles), `DS.Motion.*` (`Double` seconds and `Animation` springs). One short namespace rather than a prefix on each type name, which fits STD-swift-59 [inferred]. The proposed change: `nonisolated` on the namespace, its extension and the color helper; `public` stays, so the same file can move into a package [inferred].
platform notes: the exported colors switch on light and dark only. Increase Contrast is a separate signal in DC-L19-17 and in the house standards (STD-accessibility-motion-12, written for the web), and the Swift colors do not read it today [inferred from the engine code]; DC-L10-22 already notes that mapping onto Apple's dynamic system colors needs custom work. Swift 6.3 is the baseline; the `async` and `@concurrent` rules do not apply on Swift 6.1 or earlier, and Swift 6.4 features are not written yet (STD-swift-01) [S-L19-034]. Jetpack Compose has no house code standard (DC-L19-148).
accessibility constraints: text uses Dynamic Type text styles so it follows the person's text size (STD-accessibility-motion-13); every exported spring still needs its reduced-motion version (STD-accessibility-motion-02) [inferred application].
default: (default + heuristic) Default: the token file marked `nonisolated` wherever it goes; in the app target while there is one app, in a package once a second target needs it [inferred]; the Swift version recorded with Q-plat-09 before any Swift is written (STD-swift-01). Rule of thumb: tokens are constants, and constants should be readable from any code.
evidence: [S-L19-034]; compared with DC-L10-20, DC-L10-22, DC-L19-17, DC-L19-148, the conflicts recorded under STD-swift-17, STD-swift-18 and STD-swift-44, and `engine.py export_swift`.
maps to:
- Q-token-08: the Swift output marks its namespace, extension and color helper `nonisolated` (an engine change that resolves the three recorded conflicts).
- Q-plat-09: new follow-up field (zoom 3, show if Q-plat-08 is `swiftui`): "Which Swift version does the project build with?" Default Swift 6.3 (STD-swift-01), because which house Swift rules apply depends on it.
- Q-plat-08 `swiftui`: its "comes with" note (DC-L19-148) adds "a nonisolated Swift token file or package, and code written to the house Swift standard".
- Export skill (`opendesigner-export`): the install step becomes "Add to the app target, or to a shared package when more than one target uses the tokens" [inferred].
- Visual sample: a frame strip in which a gesture's animation starts in the synchronous callback, beside one started from a Task a frame later [S-L19-034] [inferred for the second strip].
impact now / as it grows:
- *App target, as today:* now nothing to set up. As it grows, the first background renderer or custom shape that reads a token hits a compile error, and every such read needs a workaround.
- *App target, `nonisolated`:* now one keyword in three places. As it grows, tokens stay readable from any code the app adds.
- *Shared package:* now a package, versioning and explicit access control. As it grows, apps and extensions read one source, and a token change reaches all of them in one release [inferred].
standards: STD-swift-01, STD-swift-17, STD-swift-18, STD-swift-26, STD-swift-32, STD-swift-43, STD-swift-44, STD-swift-45, STD-swift-59, STD-swift-61, STD-swift-75, STD-swift-88, STD-swift-97, STD-accessibility-motion-13

title: Sharing out of the app: the system share, share cards and the screenshot moment
block path: Platforms > Sharing > How content leaves the app
questions: (questions the designer answers) What will people want to send to someone else? Do they use the system's share button, a card the product designs for sharing, or a screenshot? On desktop, can they drag content out into other apps?
options:
- **The system share button on items:** Apple's universal share button is found on almost all Mac apps, because sometimes it is simply the handier way; the example app pairs it with its own floating action bar (copy, find, delete) [S-L19-067].
- **Drag content out (desktop):** on the Mac, drag and drop of anything anywhere is called a must: content comes in by dropping it on the app and goes out by dragging it into Figma, Finder or anywhere else [S-L19-067].
- **Share cards the product designs:** Opal turns screen-time insights into a swipeable story like an Instagram story, and data that looks that good gets shared [S-L19-110]. The Wrapped redesign keeps the share button always visible because sharing is why Wrapped succeeds, uses one share button with slide, chapter and whole-recap scopes, and puts the owner's name on shared content [S-L19-076] (DC-L19-136 treats this as a reason to come back).
- **The screenshot moment:** when someone takes a screenshot in Moonly, a ready-made flow shares it in one tap; 23% of users share something, bringing millions of free views, because people share insights about themselves, not features [S-L19-111].
- **Nothing to share:** products whose content is private or only useful inside the product [inferred].
visual effect: System share: a familiar icon and sheet, no design work. Drag out: the app feels part of the desktop [S-L19-067]. Share cards: branded, tall, content-first images that carry the product to new people [S-L19-110] [S-L19-076]. Screenshot flow: a small prompt right after the screenshot [inferred appearance].
depends on: Q-aud-02 (`consumer` and `play` products share more than `work` and `high-trust` ones [inferred]), Q-plat-01, DC-L19-136, how private the data is (STD-visual-details-41).
affects: the share button and sheet, share-card templates (brand color, type and the owner's name drawn into an image), recap and story components, desktop drag sources, a screenshot listener.
token encoding: none new; share cards reuse the brand's color and type tokens [inferred].
platform notes: the share-button and drag-out examples are macOS [S-L19-067]; the screenshot flow is in an iPhone app [S-L19-111]; story-shaped sharing is a phone pattern [S-L19-110] [S-L19-076]. No source covers sharing from the web.
accessibility constraints: the share control is a labelled button that never depends on hover (STD-accessibility-motion-15); a screenshot prompt can be dismissed and never blocks the screen (STD-accessibility-motion-24) [inferred application]; a card that shows personal data (screen time, money, health) shares only what the person chose (STD-visual-details-41) [inferred application]; text on a card keeps its contrast over any image (DC-L19-74).
default: (default + heuristic) Default `system-share` on anything a person might send; share cards only when the product's data says something about the person (recaps, progress, results); the screenshot flow only when people already screenshot those moments [inferred]. Rule of thumb: people share what says something about them [S-L19-111]; Mobbin's gut check for memorable dashboards, "Would I screenshot this, and why?" [S-L19-110], can also pick which screens deserve a share card [inferred application].
maps to:
- New question (proposed Q-plat-18, zoom 3, stage 04, show if Q-plat-01 includes `ios`, `android` or `desktop`): "What will people share out of the product, and how?" Options `system-share` (default), `share-cards`, `screenshot-flow`, `drag-out` (desktop), `none`; `share-cards` pre-selected when Q-aud-02 is `consumer` or `play` [inferred].
- Visual samples: Opal's story-shaped insights [S-L19-110]; the Wrapped share button with three scopes and the owner's name [S-L19-076]; a Mac item dragged into Finder with the share button beside it [S-L19-067].
impact now / as it grows:
- *System share:* now one icon per item. As it grows, it stays the same across every new kind of item.
- *Drag out:* now one drag source per kind of content. As it grows, each new kind needs a format other apps accept [inferred].
- *Share cards:* now one template per shareable moment. As it grows, every card carries the brand to new people, and each new card needs its privacy check [inferred].
- *Screenshot flow:* now one listener and one sheet. As it grows, it must stay rare enough not to bother people who screenshot for themselves [inferred].
- *Nothing to share:* now nothing to build. As it grows, people screenshot anyway, with no brand or name on what they send [inferred].
standards: STD-visual-details-41, STD-accessibility-motion-15, STD-accessibility-motion-24

title: Which references to learn from, and what to take from each
block path: Builder > Input > Reference intake (Stage 00; also Stage 03 product likes)
questions: (questions the designer answers) Which examples should the builder learn from: products you use, showcase shots, or competitors? What exactly do you like about each one? Should we borrow one whole page, or one section from each of several sites?
options:
- **Screenshots of shipped products:** a screenshot of a real product (Linear) gave an AI the look the author was after, while a busy Dribbble dashboard used with the same prompt lost its small details; he also suggests realistic sites from SiteInspire but did not test one [S-L19-086]. Studying the apps you use, and asking why an interaction feels good, is how taste is trained [S-L19-008]. One review of 50 software landing pages counted what recurs (41 of 50 showed customer logos) before borrowing [S-L19-066].
- **A library of shipped screens, searched by industry and flow:** Mobbin's demo has an AI study how top apps in the same industry handle one flow (onboarding and account opening across fintech and banking apps) before designing it, because a banking onboarding flow is not a generic one [S-L19-108]. The library describes itself as over 600,000 screens, 322,000 flows and 1,000 apps, its own marketing figures [S-L19-109]. It is paid, and it cannot decide what to prioritize, keep or cut [S-L19-108]. How the builder runs that research is DC-L19-178.
- **Showcase shots (Dribbble-style concepts):** they look great, but busy shots lose their small details when an AI reads them [S-L19-086]. They often favour looks over usability [S-L19-049] [S-L19-075], fall apart once each element is checked for meaning [S-L19-068], and their busy layouts distract people on a real site [S-L19-040].
- **A curated list of tastemakers:** find people respected in the field, then the people they admire, and study their designs, apps and books [S-L19-008].
- **An annotated swipe file:** collect about 20 hero and feature sections and annotate a couple for spacing, hierarchy and grouping; take a page apart into zones (text block, navbar, stats, image) before designing [S-L19-043]. One designer builds a mood board before opening Figma so he starts with a full idea, not a sliver of one [S-L19-040].
- **One section from each site ("Frankensteining"):** choose a reference for each section to work out the message and page flow, keep only the wireframe, and discard the references' visuals [S-L19-062]. Two redesigns borrow and adapt layouts from competitors and sibling products the same way [S-L19-082] [S-L19-065].
- **Competitors, flagged only:** today's Q-brand-02 option `competitors` and DC-L17-03's flag-only path.
visual effect: Shipped-product references give screens that look buildable and complete. Showcase references give dramatic screens that turn out thin or illogical once real content and states arrive, with small details dropped [S-L19-086] [S-L19-068]. Section-by-section references give a page flow fitted to the message, wearing the person's own identity [S-L19-062].
depends on: the entry path (Q-scope-05), the identity firewall (DC-L17-03).
affects: values pre-filled by `engine.py intake`, section and layout options (DC-L19-50, DC-L19-51), direction (Q-dir-01), the decision log's `reference` provenance.
token encoding: none (process decision). Pre-filled values keep DC-L17-03's provenance (`$extensions.opendesigner.source = {reference, method, confidence}`), plus a `why` string holding what the person said they like about the reference [inferred].
platform notes: web references expose computed values; app references arrive as screenshots, so their values are estimates (DC-L17-03). Kole Jain names Mobbin as a place to collect real app and site screens in videos Mobbin sponsors [S-L19-043] [S-L19-054], and Mobbin's own videos promote it [S-L19-108] [S-L19-109]; it covers mobile and web screens [S-L19-109]. Those screens are other companies' products, so the identity firewall applies to them, and no source covers the library's licence terms [inferred].
accessibility constraints: every value taken from a reference is re-checked in its new context (DC-L17-03). In one video, a Dribbble tab bar had inactive icons too faint to see and two background colors nobody could tell apart [S-L19-075], so showcase colors are never copied unchecked.
default: (default + heuristic) Default: ask for products the person uses first. Accept a showcase shot, but say it is read for mood only, not for layout or values [S-L19-086] [S-L19-068]. Heuristic: for every reference, ask one follow-up, "What do you like about it?", and record the answer as its reason, because taste means naming why something feels right [S-L19-008] [S-L19-011]. Take structure section by section, never identity (confirms DC-L17-03 and Q-ref-01's use/avoid line). Confirms DC-L18-09 (1-3 references liked and one disliked). Second heuristic: for each element carried over from a reference, ask why this product needs it. Moonly's founder asks that before copying anything other apps have; he removed the login screen, although only 12% of apps on Mobbin have no sign-up or login step anywhere [S-L19-111]. This does not undo the familiarity rule: keep the convention unless you can show something better and test it (STD-visual-details-37, DC-L13-17). Moonly reasoned through what the login was for (saved data, emails, email marketing) before removing it; the video does not say the removal itself was A/B tested [S-L19-111]. The claim that an AI cannot see a busy shot's details rests on one side-by-side test in one model [S-L19-086]; three other videos agree that showcase shots trade usability for looks [S-L19-049] [S-L19-068] [S-L19-075], so the warning holds even if the mechanism is one person's observation.
maps to:
- Q-ref-01: new option `product-screens` "Screenshots of products you use", split from `screenshot`, with the note that showcase shots are read for mood only [S-L19-086]. New option `per-section` "A different site for each section (flow only)" [S-L19-062]. New heuristic: one follow-up per reference, "What do you like about it?", saved as the reason [S-L19-008]. New heuristic: for each element carried over, ask why this product needs it [S-L19-111].
- Q-brand-02: new heuristic: after the person names products, ask why for each, and offer the answers as tie-breaker candidates for Q-brand-07 [inferred]. For the `competitors` option, a head-to-head comparison of two competitors' flows (Mobbin's example: two delivery apps' checkout, tipping and order summary) is one way to fill it [S-L19-108] [inferred].
- Visual sample: the same prompt built from a busy showcase shot and from a shipped-product screenshot [S-L19-086].
impact now / as it grows:
- *Shipped products:* now, realistic starting values and fewer invented details. As it grows, the product follows conventions people already know, which are easier to extend [S-L19-054].
- *Library of shipped screens:* now, a paid tool and one research step per flow. As it grows, each new flow starts from how shipped products in the same industry solve it (DC-L19-178).
- *Showcase shots:* now, a striking mood. As it grows, screens break as real content, states and edge cases arrive [S-L19-068].
- *Tastemaker list:* now, a slower start. As it grows, the team shares a quality bar it can point to.
- *Swipe file:* now, about 20 sections of homework. As it grows, a ready library for every new page.
- *One section from each site:* now, a page flow fitted to the message. As it grows, pages only feel like one product if identity is defined separately from layout (DC-L19-162) [S-L19-062].
